Collecting: clause 1 is step 2.1, clause 2 is step 1.3, clause 3 is step 1.4, and clause 4 follows from steps 1.5 and 2.2 in the two directions; this proves the statement.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement fixes N>=1 and an actual curve on a nonempty open interval J when asserting the motion equivalences. Such a curve supplies phase points; if a configuration domain admits no points there is no such curve and these conditional claims are vacuous. Step 2.2 uses the full momentum fibre over each actual x, which contains the explicitly specified zero momentum p=0, to define g(t,x)=f(t,x,0). It selects no element from an empty fibre.

The Statement for the forced Hamiltonian field imposes no nonzero phase-value condition: zero momentum and zero tangent values are allowed at admissible base points, and its algebraic formulas apply there. A zero configuration is included only when it lies in the declared chart, so no origin outside the domain is claimed.
Statement allows N=1 and steps 1.1–1.4 use the same three-component Cartesian field and forced momentum equations; a one-coordinate immersion separately yields the scalar chart equation of step 1.3.

Statement clause 4 requires an exact velocity-independent residual potential on Q, not mere independence of velocity. Step 2.2 proves necessity with V=g-U and identifies the componentwise additive time freedom; step 1.5 proves sufficiency. Nonexact closed residual forces therefore remain excluded.

boundaries.reason: The Statement for the forced Hamiltonian field is local on its declared chart and time domain; it makes no terminal boundary-value prescription or extension outside that domain.
Step 2.2 constructs the residual potential as g-U with g(t,x)=f(t,x,0); no primitives are chosen on unrelated domains. Component-dependent time additions are precisely the declared gauge freedom.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1–1.4 and 2.1 identify the motion, momentum and integral-curve formulations. In clause 4, step 2.2 takes a Hamiltonian forced field to the exact residual potential V=g-U, with componentwise time gauge freedom.

Steps 1.1–1.4 express the Hamilton systems back as the model and Lagrange equations. For clause 4, step 1.5 starts with the exact residual potential and constructs f=H+V, whose field is exactly the forced field.

risk_review.notes: Read all eight steps and exact CM12 hyperregularity/equivalence, motions, potential-normalization, field and zero-derivative supplier statements. Clauses 1-3 retain their independent hypotheses: d=0 for unforced motions, declared Lagrange equations for any immersion rather than unconstrained ambient equations. Necessity in clause 4 integrates the p-gradient on the entire convex momentum fiber and sets g(t,x)=f(t,x,0), preserving joint C2 regularity; V=g-U is global and velocity independent. Sufficiency uses H+V. Gauge functions are independent on open connected components; no closed-to-exact assertion or existence/completeness claim. Reader joint-C2 convention makes the quantified phase function explicit without changing autonomous consumer uses.

citations.quote:
Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the
momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]], the canonical
coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]] and the Hamiltonian fields of
[[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]]. Dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]];
differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) Phase functions.** Let $W_{0}$ be a nonempty open subset of a phase
domain of the presentation. A **phase function of the presentation on
$W_{0}$ of class $C^{k}$** is a map $f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{k}$
($k\ge1$); its physical reading is a model quantity computed from the
positions and momenta of the labels, and its dimension is declared as part of
the datum. A **time-dependent phase function** on an interval $J\subseteq
I_{0}$ is a map $f:J\times W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ of the declared class, written
$f_{t}:=f(t,\cdot)$.

**(b) The bracket.** For $C^1$ phase functions $f,g:W_0\to\mathbb R$, define their **Poisson bracket for the presentation** by the pointwise coordinate formula $\{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g$ in a canonical chart, in the finite-regularity convention of [[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]]. This is a continuous function. The definition is independent of the canonical chart: for a canonical $C^1$ coordinate change with derivative $M$, the matrix identity implies $MJM^{\mathsf T}=J$, and the equivalence of the two matrix identities is proved in [[prop-cm-canonical-map-tests-and-hamiltonian-transport]], and the chain rule transforms the two gradients so their pairing is unchanged.

When both functions are $C^2$, their Hamiltonian fields of [[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]] are $C^1$, and the bracket has the intrinsic formula
$$\{f,g\}=\omega(X_f,X_g)=df(X_g)=X_g(f)=-X_f(g).$$
In this case it is $C^1$, with the same sign convention as the smooth root bracket and [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]. The extension to $C^1$ inputs makes evolution identities for $C^1$ observables and nested brackets of $C^2$ functions meaningful; it does not assert closure of the $C^2$ class under the bracket. Its dimension is $[f][g](\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1})^{-1}$, the product of the entries' dimensions divided by the action dimension of the two-form.

**(c) Coordinate formula.** In the Cartesian canonical coordinates $(x,p)$
of the presentation, and more generally in any canonical chart
$(\theta^{1},\dots,\theta^{2m})$ of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]],

$$\{f,g\}=\sum_{a=1}^{3N}\Bigl(f_{x^{a}}g_{p_{a}}-f_{p_{a}}g_{x^{a}}\Bigr)=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g,\qquad \{f,g\}=\sum_{a=1}^{m}\Bigl(f_{\theta^{a}}g_{\theta^{m+a}}-f_{\theta^{m+a}}g_{\theta^{a}}\Bigr),$$

with derivatives those of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. The coordinate formula is
recorded here and its identities (bilinearity, skew-symmetry, the Leibniz
rule, the Jacobi identity and the fundamental brackets) are proved in the
bracket-identities theorem of this page.

**(d) Status.** The item defines a bilinear operation on the declared phase
domain by the pointwise coordinate formula, and for $C^2$ entries by $\{f,g\}=\omega(X_f,X_g)$, hence
independently of the canonical chart used to evaluate the coordinate
formula. It asserts no equation of motion, no conservation law, no algebraic
identity beyond well-definedness and no measured value; in particular the
bracket with the Hamiltonian and the notion of first integral are the subject
of the evolution theorem of this page.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the
momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]] and the canonical
coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]]: the Cartesian phase domain
$W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$, its two-form $\omega$, a generalized-coordinate
chart map $\Phi_{X}$ and the form $\omega_{X}$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]); the presentation is
hyperregular on every chart with the Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]] and [[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]],

$$H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x),\qquad \widetilde H(t,q,P)=\tfrac12\,P\cdot G(q)^{-1}P+\widetilde U(t,q).$$

Differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and gradients those of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

**(a) The field of a phase function.** Let $W_{0}\subseteq W$ be nonempty
open and let $f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^{2}$. By clause 1 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] the form $\omega$ is nondegenerate on
$W_{0}$, so there is exactly one $C^{1}$ vector field $X_{f}$ on $W_{0}$ with

$$\iota_{X_{f}}\omega=df$$

(the sign convention of [[def-hamiltonian-vector-field-and-hamiltonian-function]]
and [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]); it
is the **Hamiltonian field of $f$ for the presentation**. In the Cartesian
coordinates $(x,p)$, writing $\nabla f=(f_{x^{1}},\dots,f_{x^{3N}},f_{p_{1}},\dots,f_{p_{3N}})$,

$$X_{f}=\bigl(f_{p},\,-f_{x}\bigr)=J\nabla f,\qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0_{3N}&I_{3N}\\-I_{3N}&0_{3N}\end{pmatrix};$$

in any canonical chart $(\theta^{1},\dots,\theta^{2m})$ of the presentation
the same field reads $X_{f}=\bigl(f_{\theta^{m+1}},\dots,f_{\theta^{2m}},-f_{\theta^{1}},\dots,-f_{\theta^{m}}\bigr)$.
A vector field on $W_{0}$ is called **Hamiltonian for the presentation** when
it is $X_{f}$ for some $C^{2}$ function $f$; in particular
$X_{f}=0$ exactly when $f$ is locally constant on $W_{0}$. Vector fields are
read as tangent-bundle sections of
[[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]].

**(b) The field of the branch Hamiltonian.** For each $t\in I_{0}$ the
function $H_{t}:=H(t,\cdot)$ is $C^{2}$ on $W$, and the **Hamiltonian field
of the presentation** at time $t$ is $X_{H_{t}}$:

$$X_{H_{t}}(x,p)=\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,\ -\nabla_{x}U(t,x)\bigr),$$

whose components are a velocity and a force. In the coordinates $X$ the
corresponding field is
$X_{\widetilde H_{t}}(q,P)=\bigl(G(q)^{-1}P,\ -\partial_{q}\widetilde H(t,q,P)\bigr)$,
where the second slot retains the kinetic contribution
$-\tfrac12P\cdot\partial_{q}(G(q)^{-1})P$ when the metric varies. If
$d\not\equiv0$ the model's forced evolution carries the additional momentum
source $d$; the corresponding vector field
$(x,p)\mapsto\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,-\nabla_{x}U(t,x)+d(t,x,\mathsf M^{-1}p)\bigr)$
is generally not a Hamiltonian field for the presentation, and it is one
exactly when the residual force has a potential independent of the velocity
slot (the criterion is proved in clause 4 of the corresponding theorem of this
page).

**(c) Time dependence and status.** For a time-dependent $H$ the assignment
$t\mapsto X_{H_{t}}$ is a time-dependent field on the phase domain; each
$X_{H_{t}}$ is $C^{1}$, hence locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and no
completeness of its integral curves is asserted here. The item defines the
field datum and its chart expressions; the identification of the model's
motions with the integral curves, and all conservation or invariance
properties, are the subject of the other items of this page. The field is
defined by the intrinsic equation $\iota_{X}\omega=dH$ and therefore does not
depend on the canonical chart used to compute it.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ and nonempty open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$,
a $C^{2}$ potential $U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ of dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing regularity
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]], the Euclidean product on $\mathbb R^{3N}$ is
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Write $n:=3N\ge1$. The
Cartesian momentum phase chart of the presentation is
$I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with the momentum $p=\mathsf Mv$ of
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]], and the momentum phase chart of a
generalized-coordinate map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates is
$I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ with the generalized momentum
$P=G(q)v$, $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]).

**(a) Cartesian chart.** The **Cartesian phase domain of the presentation** is
the nonempty open set

$$W:=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n},\qquad z=(x,p),$$

a phase domain in the sense of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]
(openness is clause (a) of [[def-cm01-configuration]]; nonemptiness is an
explicit hypothesis here, so an empty configuration domain has no instances
of this phase-domain definition). On $W$ the
**canonical one-form of the presentation in the Cartesian chart** is the smooth
one-form

$$\lambda_{(x,p)}(\delta x,\delta p):=p\cdot\delta x\qquad\bigl((x,p)\in W,\ (\delta x,\delta p)\in\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}\bigr),$$

where $p\cdot\delta x$ is the Euclidean pairing of the momentum covector with
the displacement, and the **two-form of the presentation in the Cartesian
chart** is

$$\omega:=-d\lambda$$

([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]). In coordinates, reading
$x=(x^{1},\dots,x^{3N})$ and $p=(p_{1},\dots,p_{3N})$ as the standard
coordinates of $W$,

$$\lambda=\sum_{a=1}^{3N}p_{a}\,dx^{a},\qquad \omega=\sum_{a=1}^{3N}dx^{a}\wedge dp_{a},\qquad \omega_{(x,p)}\bigl((\delta x,\delta p),(\delta x',\delta p')\bigr)=\delta x\cdot\delta p'-\delta p\cdot\delta x',$$

the last identity using the Euclidean product. The dimension of both forms is
that of action, $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$: the pairing of a momentum
($\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$) with a displacement ($\ell$). The forms have no
explicit time dependence; for each $t\in I_{0}$ the slice $\{t\}\times W$
carries the same two-form. The momentum phase chart with time,
$I_{0}\times W$ with coordinates $(t,x,p)$, is the domain of the Hamiltonians
and fields of this page. The **sign convention** fixed by
[[def-hamiltonian-vector-field-and-hamiltonian-function]] and used
throughout is $\iota_{X}\omega=dH$; $H$ denotes a phase function as in that
item.

**(b) Generalized-coordinate chart.** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
generalized-coordinate map with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$ and
kinetic metric $G$, and let $r$ be its number of coordinates
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]). The **chart map of the
presentation in the coordinates $X$** is

$$\Phi_{X}:\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Phi_{X}(q,P):=\Bigl(X(q),\ \mathsf M\,DX(q)\,G(q)^{-1}P\Bigr).$$

Here $DX(q)$ is the $(3N)\times r$ Jacobian of $X$ at $q$
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]), $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$
is symmetric positive definite ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]],
[[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]), and $P$ is a
generalized momentum. The image of $\Phi_{X}$ is

$$\Phi_{X}(\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r})=\bigl\{\,(X(q),\mathsf M\,DX(q)v)\ :\ q\in\Omega,\ v\in\mathbb R^{r}\,\bigr\},$$

the momentum chart of the presentation in the coordinates $X$; indeed
$P\mapsto v=G(q)^{-1}P$ is a linear bijection of $\mathbb R^{r}$. The map
$\Phi_X$ is $C^2$: $X$ is $C^3$, so $DX$ is $C^2$; hence
$G=DX^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M DX$ is $C^2$, and $G^{-1}$ is $C^2$ because
matrix inversion is given by the adjugate divided by the nonvanishing
determinant on the positive-definite matrices. The fiber
coefficient $\mathsf M DX(q)G(q)^{-1}$ is $C^2$. Thus $\Phi_X$ is a
$C^2$ immersion:
its derivative is injective at every point, because $DX(q)$ is injective
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-euclidean-submersions-and-immersions]]) and $P\mapsto G(q)^{-1}P$ is a
linear bijection; when $r=3N$ its derivative is invertible and it is a local
$C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its open image in $W$
(equivalently $\mathsf M\,DX(q)G(q)^{-1}=DX(q)^{-\mathsf T}$: see the
recorded identity below). We use the pointwise coordinate pullback: for a smooth
$k$-form $\eta$ on $W$, set
$(\Phi_X^*\eta)_{(q,P)}(v_1,\dots,v_k):=
\eta_{\Phi_X(q,P)}(D\Phi_X(q,P)v_1,\dots,D\Phi_X(q,P)v_k)$, extending the
formula of [[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]] to this $C^2$ map. The
result has continuous coefficients. The **forms of the presentation in the
coordinates $X$** are

$$\lambda_{X}:=\Phi_{X}^{*}\lambda,\qquad \omega_{X}:=\Phi_{X}^{*}\omega$$

([[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]]). In the coordinates $(q,P)$ on
$\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ the following identities hold, and are proved in
clause 2 of the symplectic-structure theorem of this page:

$$\lambda_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}P_{a}\,dq^{a},\qquad \omega_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}dq^{a}\wedge dP_{a};$$

moreover, when $r=3N$ and $DX(q)$ is invertible,
$\mathsf M\,DX(q)G(q)^{-1}=DX(q)^{-\mathsf T}$, so that on an open
generalized-coordinate chart the chart map reads
$\Phi_X(q,P)=\bigl(X(q),DX(q)^{-\mathsf T}P\bigr)$ and the chart transition
between the two descriptions of the same momentum datum is a $C^2$ local
diffeomorphism.

**(c) Status.** The item defines the two-form datum of the declared
presentation on its declared charts, together with the sign convention for
fields. It asserts no closedness, no nondegeneracy, no equation of motion, no
conservation law and no measured value; those are the subject of the other
items of this page. The forms depend on the declared chart and its coordinate
dimensions, but not on the residual forces $d$ nor on the normalization
$U\mapsto U+c(t)$ of the potential representative. All objects are model
objects of the idealization declared by the force branch.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
momentum charts, the phase domains and the two-form datum of
[[def-cm13-two-form]]: the Cartesian phase domain $W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$
with $n=3N$, its two-form $\omega$, and for each generalized-coordinate map
$X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates the chart map $\Phi_{X}$ and the form
$\omega_{X}$ ([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]], [[def-cm01-configuration]]). All
differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) Canonical coordinates.** Let $W_{0}\subseteq W$ (or
$W_{0}\subseteq\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$) be nonempty open, and let

$$\theta=(\theta^{1},\dots,\theta^{2m}):W_{0}\longrightarrow V\subseteq\mathbb R^{2m}$$

be a $C^{1}$ chart of $W_{0}$ onto an open set $V$ ([[def-metric-topology]]),
with $m$ the half-dimension of $W_{0}$. Write $\sigma=\omega|_{W_0}$ and $\alpha=\lambda|_{W_0}$ in the Cartesian case, and $\sigma=\omega_X|_{W_0}$ and $\alpha=\lambda_X|_{W_0}$ in the generalized-coordinate case. Each coordinate $\theta^a$ has a declared dimension $\eta_a$ and unit; its paired coordinate $\theta^{m+a}$ has dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}\eta_a^{-1}$ and a declared compatible unit, so every summand below has action dimension. Coordinate formulas use the numerical representatives in these fixed units. The coordinates $\theta$ are
**canonical coordinates for the presentation's two-form** on $W_{0}$ when the
two-form takes the **canonical form**

$$\sigma=\sum_{a=1}^{m}d\theta^{a}\wedge d\theta^{m+a}$$

pointwise on $W_{0}$, using the finite-coordinate form and pullback conventions of [[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]]; equivalently, when the
pullback identity $\theta^{*}\omega_{V}^{\mathrm{st}}=\sigma$ holds
for the standard two-form $\omega_{V}^{\mathrm{st}}$ of $V$
([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]],
[[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]]), equivalently when
$D\theta(z)^{\mathsf T}J\,D\theta(z)=J$ for the standard symplectic matrix
$J$ at every $z\in W_{0}$
([[prop-cm-canonical-map-tests-and-hamiltonian-transport]]). A **canonical
chart of the presentation** is a chart whose coordinates are canonical in
this sense; the equivalence with the canonical maps defined later on this
page is recorded with those definitions.

**(b) The model's own charts are canonical.** The Cartesian coordinates
$(x,p)$ on $W$ are canonical coordinates: by clause 1 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] the two-form is
$\omega=\sum_{a}dx^{a}\wedge dp_{a}$. For a generalized-coordinate map, the
coordinates $(q,P)$ on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ are canonical coordinates
for the pulled-back form $\omega_{X}$: by clause 2 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] one has
$\omega_{X}=\sum_{a}dq^{a}\wedge dP_{a}$, and when the map is a genuine chart
($r=3N$) the chart transition is a change of canonical coordinates on
overlaps.

**(c) Canonical one-form up to gauge at classical differentiability.** For a $C^2$ canonical chart $\theta$, the source canonical one-form $\alpha$ specified in clause (a) from
[[def-cm13-two-form]] is said to be **in canonical form up to gauge** in the
canonical coordinates $\theta$ when the difference
$\alpha-\sum_{a}\theta^{m+a}d\theta^{a}$ is a closed one-form on $W_{0}$;
exactness of that difference is not required. For the presentation's own
charts the difference of the two canonical one-forms is closed by clause 3 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]]. These charts are $C^2$ or smoother. For a merely $C^1$ chart clause (a) retains its full pointwise meaning, but the coefficients of the pulled-back one-form may be only continuous, so this clause does not apply the classical exterior derivative to them.

**(d) Status and warnings.** The item defines a coordinate condition on a
declared chart and records the one fact that the presentation's own momentum
charts satisfy it. It asserts no existence of canonical coordinates beyond
the model's charts, no global statement on multiply connected phase domains,
no dynamics and no measured value. A chart that is merely a diffeomorphism
need not be canonical; the determinant test
$|\det D\theta|=1$ is necessary but, in dimension $2m\ge4$, not sufficient
for canonicity (the scope remark of this page records the witness).

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data, charts and forms of [[def-cm13-two-form]]: masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$,
open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ and mass operator
$\mathsf M$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), time window $I_{0}$, $C^{2}$
potential $U$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing regularity
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], [[def-cm01-units]]), the Cartesian phase
domain $W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with $n=3N$, its canonical one-form
$\lambda$ and two-form $\omega=-d\lambda$, and for each generalized-coordinate
map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates and kinetic metric $G$ the chart map
$\Phi_{X}(q,P)=(X(q),\mathsf M\,DX(q)G(q)^{-1}P)$ with pullbacks
$\lambda_{X}=\Phi_{X}^{*}\lambda$ and $\omega_{X}=\Phi_{X}^{*}\omega$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]], [[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]). Then:

1. **(Cartesian chart)** $\omega$ is the standard two-form of the phase
   domain $W$ in the sense of
   [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]: $d\omega=0$ and
   $\omega$ is nondegenerate at every point of $W$; hence $(W,\omega)$ is a
   symplectic manifold in the sense of
   [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]].
2. **(generalized-coordinate chart)** On $\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$,

$$\lambda_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}P_{a}\,dq^{a},\qquad \omega_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}dq^{a}\wedge dP_{a};$$

   consequently $\omega_{X}$ is closed and nondegenerate at every point, so
   $\Phi_{X}^{*}\omega$ is the standard two-form of the phase domain
   $\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ and $\Phi_{X}$ preserves the two-form.
3. **(full-dimensional chart transitions)** Let $X_1,X_2$ be generalized-coordinate
   charts with $r=3N$, and restrict their momentum chart maps to neighborhoods
   on which each $\Phi_{X_j}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of the
   Cartesian phase domain. On every overlap of those image neighborhoods,
   the genuine phase-chart transition
   $\Theta=\Phi_{X_2}^{-1}\circ\Phi_{X_1}$ preserves the two-form. The
   difference $\lambda_{X_1}-\Theta^*\lambda_{X_2}$ is a closed one-form
   there; no exactness is asserted. Lower-dimensional generalized-coordinate
   immersions have the symplectic pullback form of clause 2, but are not
   transitions between open full-dimensional phase charts.

The statement is a conditional deduction from the adopted force branch, the
declared presentation and the cited mathematics. It asserts no equation of
motion, no conservation law, no completeness of any flow and no empirical
content.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with standard two-form
$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]), and let
$H:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Write
$\nabla H=(H_{q^1},\dots,H_{q^n},H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n})$ for the Euclidean gradient
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and $J$ for the standard symplectic matrix. Then:

1. there is exactly one $C^1$ vector field $X_H$ on $U$ with $\iota_{X_H}\omega_U=dH$, and it is
   $$X_H=J\nabla H=\bigl(H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n},-H_{q^1},\dots,-H_{q^n}\bigr);$$
2. an integral curve $t\mapsto(q(t),p(t))$ of $X_H$ satisfies Hamilton's equations
   $$\dot q^i=H_{p_i}(q,p),\qquad \dot p_i=-H_{q^i}(q,p)\qquad(i=1,\dots,n);$$
3. for $f,g\in C^2(U)$ the Poisson bracket
   $\{f,g\}:=\omega_U(X_f,X_g)$ (in the finite-regularity convention of [[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]]) is
   $$\{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(f_{q^i}g_{p_i}-f_{p_i}g_{q^i}\bigr),$$
   hence $\{f,g\}=-\{g,f\}$, and $\{f,g\}$ is $C^1$ on $U$.

For $F,G\in C^\infty(M)$, the **Poisson bracket** in the library convention is

$$\{F,G\}:=\omega(X_F,X_G)=dF(X_G)=X_G(F)=-X_F(G).$$

All four formulas use $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$. In particular, the order in the
observable formula is important: evolution by $H$ differentiates $F$ as
$X_H(F)=\{F,H\}$.
For a $C^2$ scalar field $f$, $H_f(a)^T=H_f(a)$ at every point $a$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. The exterior derivative is an
$\mathbb R$-linear map $d:\Omega^*(M)\to\Omega^*(M)$ of degree one.
For homogeneous smooth forms $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M)$ and
$\beta\in\Omega^q(M)$, $$d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{\deg\alpha}\alpha\wedge d\beta.$$

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the **transpose** of $A$ is the matrix
$A^{\mathsf T}\in M_{n\times m}(F)$ defined by

$$(A^{\mathsf T})_{ji}:=a_{ij}.$$

Thus transposition interchanges rows and columns. The transpose of a zero-sized
matrix is the unique matrix of the transposed zero-sized shape.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2] the bracket satisfies $\{f,g\}=df(X_{g})=-dg(X_{f})$, and $\alpha X_{f}+\beta X_{g}=X_{\alpha f+\beta g}$ because $\iota_{X}\omega=d(\cdot)$ is linear and $\omega$ is bilinear; since $\omega$ is antisymmetric, $\{f,g\}=\omega(X_{f},X_{g})=-\omega(X_{g},X_{f})=-\{g,f\}$ and $\{f,f\}=0$; the coordinate formula of [F2] displays the same statements, proving clause 1 and the first identity of clause 4.

Hessian lemma: for $C^{2}$ functions $u,v$, the gradient of $\{u,v\}$ is $\mathrm{Hess}(u)J
abla v-\mathrm{Hess}(v)J
abla u$; indeed the $i$-th partial derivative of $(
abla u)^{\mathsf T}J
abla v$ is $\sum_{k,l}(u_{z^{k}z^{i}}J^{kl}v_{z^{l}}+u_{z^{k}}J^{kl}v_{z^{l}z^{i}})$, and by symmetry of the Hessians [F2] and $J^{\mathsf T}=-J$ [F3] this equals the $i$-th component of $\mathrm{Hess}(u)J
abla v-\mathrm{Hess}(v)J
abla u$.

Fundamental brackets: in a canonical chart the two-form is $\omega=\sum_{a}d\theta^{a}\wedge d\theta^{m+a}$ by [F1], and the coordinate formula of [F2] applied to the coordinate functions gives $\{\theta^{i},\theta^{j}\}=\sum_{a}(\delta^{i}_{a}\delta^{j}_{m+a}-\delta^{i}_{m+a}\delta^{j}_{a})=J^{ij}$; in the Cartesian chart $J$ is the standard matrix, so $\{x^{a},x^{b}\}=\{p_{a},p_{b}\}=0$ and $\{x^{a},p_{b}\}=\delta^{a}_{b}$; this is clause 5.

Leibniz: by [F1] and the derivation property of $d$ of [F3], $\{f,gh\}=-d(gh)(X_{f})=-g\,dh(X_{f})-h\,dg(X_{f})=g\{f,h\}+h\{f,g\}$, and the second identity follows from skew-symmetry of step 1.1 applied to the first; this proves clause 2.

Jacobi: substituting the Hessian lemma of step 1.2 into the cyclic sum and using $\{f,g\}=
abla f^{\mathsf T}J
abla g$ gives $\{f,\{g,h\}\}+\{g,\{h,f\}\}+\{h,\{f,g\}\}=(
abla f)^{\mathsf T}J\,\mathrm{Hess}(g)J
abla h-(
abla f)^{\mathsf T}J\,\mathrm{Hess}(h)J
abla g+(
abla g)^{\mathsf T}J\,\mathrm{Hess}(h)J
abla f-(
abla g)^{\mathsf T}J\,\mathrm{Hess}(f)J
abla h+(
abla h)^{\mathsf T}J\,\mathrm{Hess}(f)J
abla g-(
abla h)^{\mathsf T}J\,\mathrm{Hess}(g)J
abla f$; each scalar term is its own transpose, and transposing $(
abla f)^{\mathsf T}J\,\mathrm{Hess}(g)J
abla h$ gives $(
abla h)^{\mathsf T}J^{\mathsf T}\mathrm{Hess}(g)^{\mathsf T}J^{\mathsf T}
abla f=(
abla h)^{\mathsf T}J\,\mathrm{Hess}(g)J
abla f$ using the symmetry of the Hessian and $J^{\mathsf T}=-J$ [F2, F3]; hence the two $\mathrm{Hess}(g)$-terms differ by a sign and cancel, and the same cancellation applies to the $\mathrm{Hess}(h)$- and $\mathrm{Hess}(f)$-terms, so the cyclic sum vanishes; this is clause 3.

Collection: clause 1 is step 1.1, clause 2 is step 2.1, clause 3 is step 2.2, clause 4 is the coordinate formula of [F2] together with step 1.1, and clause 5 is step 1.3; these identities hold at the stated finite regularities with nested brackets read through the $C^1$ coordinate extension. For smooth inputs every bracket and product remains smooth, so the identities supply a Poisson algebra on $C^\infty(W_0)$.
