Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ and nonempty open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$,
a $C^{2}$ potential $U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ of dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing regularity
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]], the Euclidean product on $\mathbb R^{3N}$ is
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Write $n:=3N\ge1$. The
Cartesian momentum phase chart of the presentation is
$I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with the momentum $p=\mathsf Mv$ of
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]], and the momentum phase chart of a
generalized-coordinate map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates is
$I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ with the generalized momentum
$P=G(q)v$, $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]).

**(a) Cartesian chart.** The **Cartesian phase domain of the presentation** is
the nonempty open set

$$W:=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n},\qquad z=(x,p),$$

a phase domain in the sense of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]
(openness is clause (a) of [[def-cm01-configuration]]; nonemptiness is an
explicit hypothesis here, so an empty configuration domain has no instances
of this phase-domain definition). On $W$ the
**canonical one-form of the presentation in the Cartesian chart** is the smooth
one-form

$$\lambda_{(x,p)}(\delta x,\delta p):=p\cdot\delta x\qquad\bigl((x,p)\in W,\ (\delta x,\delta p)\in\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}\bigr),$$

where $p\cdot\delta x$ is the Euclidean pairing of the momentum covector with
the displacement, and the **two-form of the presentation in the Cartesian
chart** is

$$\omega:=-d\lambda$$

([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]). In coordinates, reading
$x=(x^{1},\dots,x^{3N})$ and $p=(p_{1},\dots,p_{3N})$ as the standard
coordinates of $W$,

$$\lambda=\sum_{a=1}^{3N}p_{a}\,dx^{a},\qquad \omega=\sum_{a=1}^{3N}dx^{a}\wedge dp_{a},\qquad \omega_{(x,p)}\bigl((\delta x,\delta p),(\delta x',\delta p')\bigr)=\delta x\cdot\delta p'-\delta p\cdot\delta x',$$

the last identity using the Euclidean product. The dimension of both forms is
that of action, $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$: the pairing of a momentum
($\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$) with a displacement ($\ell$). The forms have no
explicit time dependence; for each $t\in I_{0}$ the slice $\{t\}\times W$
carries the same two-form. The momentum phase chart with time,
$I_{0}\times W$ with coordinates $(t,x,p)$, is the domain of the Hamiltonians
and fields of this page. The **sign convention** fixed by
[[def-hamiltonian-vector-field-and-hamiltonian-function]] and used
throughout is $\iota_{X}\omega=dH$; $H$ denotes a phase function as in that
item.

**(b) Generalized-coordinate chart.** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
generalized-coordinate map with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$ and
kinetic metric $G$, and let $r$ be its number of coordinates
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]). The **chart map of the
presentation in the coordinates $X$** is

$$\Phi_{X}:\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Phi_{X}(q,P):=\Bigl(X(q),\ \mathsf M\,DX(q)\,G(q)^{-1}P\Bigr).$$

Here $DX(q)$ is the $(3N)\times r$ Jacobian of $X$ at $q$
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]), $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$
is symmetric positive definite ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]],
[[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]), and $P$ is a
generalized momentum. The image of $\Phi_{X}$ is

$$\Phi_{X}(\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r})=\bigl\{\,(X(q),\mathsf M\,DX(q)v)\ :\ q\in\Omega,\ v\in\mathbb R^{r}\,\bigr\},$$

the momentum chart of the presentation in the coordinates $X$; indeed
$P\mapsto v=G(q)^{-1}P$ is a linear bijection of $\mathbb R^{r}$. The map
$\Phi_X$ is $C^2$: $X$ is $C^3$, so $DX$ is $C^2$; hence
$G=DX^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M DX$ is $C^2$, and $G^{-1}$ is $C^2$ because
matrix inversion is given by the adjugate divided by the nonvanishing
determinant on the positive-definite matrices. The fiber
coefficient $\mathsf M DX(q)G(q)^{-1}$ is $C^2$. Thus $\Phi_X$ is a
$C^2$ immersion:
its derivative is injective at every point, because $DX(q)$ is injective
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-euclidean-submersions-and-immersions]]) and $P\mapsto G(q)^{-1}P$ is a
linear bijection; when $r=3N$ its derivative is invertible and it is a local
$C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its open image in $W$
(equivalently $\mathsf M\,DX(q)G(q)^{-1}=DX(q)^{-\mathsf T}$: see the
recorded identity below). We use the pointwise coordinate pullback: for a smooth
$k$-form $\eta$ on $W$, set
$(\Phi_X^*\eta)_{(q,P)}(v_1,\dots,v_k):=
\eta_{\Phi_X(q,P)}(D\Phi_X(q,P)v_1,\dots,D\Phi_X(q,P)v_k)$, extending the
formula of [[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]] to this $C^2$ map. The
result has continuous coefficients. The **forms of the presentation in the
coordinates $X$** are

$$\lambda_{X}:=\Phi_{X}^{*}\lambda,\qquad \omega_{X}:=\Phi_{X}^{*}\omega$$

([[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]]). In the coordinates $(q,P)$ on
$\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ the following identities hold, and are proved in
clause 2 of the symplectic-structure theorem of this page:

$$\lambda_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}P_{a}\,dq^{a},\qquad \omega_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}dq^{a}\wedge dP_{a};$$

moreover, when $r=3N$ and $DX(q)$ is invertible,
$\mathsf M\,DX(q)G(q)^{-1}=DX(q)^{-\mathsf T}$, so that on an open
generalized-coordinate chart the chart map reads
$\Phi_X(q,P)=\bigl(X(q),DX(q)^{-\mathsf T}P\bigr)$ and the chart transition
between the two descriptions of the same momentum datum is a $C^2$ local
diffeomorphism.

**(c) Status.** The item defines the two-form datum of the declared
presentation on its declared charts, together with the sign convention for
fields. It asserts no closedness, no nondegeneracy, no equation of motion, no
conservation law and no measured value; those are the subject of the other
items of this page. The forms depend on the declared chart and its coordinate
dimensions, but not on the residual forces $d$ nor on the normalization
$U\mapsto U+c(t)$ of the potential representative. All objects are model
objects of the idealization declared by the force branch.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data, charts and forms of [[def-cm13-two-form]]: masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$,
open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ and mass operator
$\mathsf M$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), time window $I_{0}$, $C^{2}$
potential $U$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing regularity
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], [[def-cm01-units]]), the Cartesian phase
domain $W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with $n=3N$, its canonical one-form
$\lambda$ and two-form $\omega=-d\lambda$, and for each generalized-coordinate
map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates and kinetic metric $G$ the chart map
$\Phi_{X}(q,P)=(X(q),\mathsf M\,DX(q)G(q)^{-1}P)$ with pullbacks
$\lambda_{X}=\Phi_{X}^{*}\lambda$ and $\omega_{X}=\Phi_{X}^{*}\omega$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]], [[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]). Then:

1. **(Cartesian chart)** $\omega$ is the standard two-form of the phase
   domain $W$ in the sense of
   [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]: $d\omega=0$ and
   $\omega$ is nondegenerate at every point of $W$; hence $(W,\omega)$ is a
   symplectic manifold in the sense of
   [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]].
2. **(generalized-coordinate chart)** On $\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$,

$$\lambda_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}P_{a}\,dq^{a},\qquad \omega_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}dq^{a}\wedge dP_{a};$$

   consequently $\omega_{X}$ is closed and nondegenerate at every point, so
   $\Phi_{X}^{*}\omega$ is the standard two-form of the phase domain
   $\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ and $\Phi_{X}$ preserves the two-form.
3. **(full-dimensional chart transitions)** Let $X_1,X_2$ be generalized-coordinate
   charts with $r=3N$, and restrict their momentum chart maps to neighborhoods
   on which each $\Phi_{X_j}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of the
   Cartesian phase domain. On every overlap of those image neighborhoods,
   the genuine phase-chart transition
   $\Theta=\Phi_{X_2}^{-1}\circ\Phi_{X_1}$ preserves the two-form. The
   difference $\lambda_{X_1}-\Theta^*\lambda_{X_2}$ is a closed one-form
   there; no exactness is asserted. Lower-dimensional generalized-coordinate
   immersions have the symplectic pullback form of clause 2, but are not
   transitions between open full-dimensional phase charts.

The statement is a conditional deduction from the adopted force branch, the
declared presentation and the cited mathematics. It asserts no equation of
motion, no conservation law, no completeness of any flow and no empirical
content.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the
momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]] and the canonical
coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]]: the Cartesian phase domain
$W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$, its two-form $\omega$, a generalized-coordinate
chart map $\Phi_{X}$ and the form $\omega_{X}$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]); the presentation is
hyperregular on every chart with the Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]] and [[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]],

$$H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x),\qquad \widetilde H(t,q,P)=\tfrac12\,P\cdot G(q)^{-1}P+\widetilde U(t,q).$$

Differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and gradients those of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

**(a) The field of a phase function.** Let $W_{0}\subseteq W$ be nonempty
open and let $f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^{2}$. By clause 1 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]] the form $\omega$ is nondegenerate on
$W_{0}$, so there is exactly one $C^{1}$ vector field $X_{f}$ on $W_{0}$ with

$$\iota_{X_{f}}\omega=df$$

(the sign convention of [[def-hamiltonian-vector-field-and-hamiltonian-function]]
and [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]); it
is the **Hamiltonian field of $f$ for the presentation**. In the Cartesian
coordinates $(x,p)$, writing $\nabla f=(f_{x^{1}},\dots,f_{x^{3N}},f_{p_{1}},\dots,f_{p_{3N}})$,

$$X_{f}=\bigl(f_{p},\,-f_{x}\bigr)=J\nabla f,\qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0_{3N}&I_{3N}\\-I_{3N}&0_{3N}\end{pmatrix};$$

in any canonical chart $(\theta^{1},\dots,\theta^{2m})$ of the presentation
the same field reads $X_{f}=\bigl(f_{\theta^{m+1}},\dots,f_{\theta^{2m}},-f_{\theta^{1}},\dots,-f_{\theta^{m}}\bigr)$.
A vector field on $W_{0}$ is called **Hamiltonian for the presentation** when
it is $X_{f}$ for some $C^{2}$ function $f$; in particular
$X_{f}=0$ exactly when $f$ is locally constant on $W_{0}$. Vector fields are
read as tangent-bundle sections of
[[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]].

**(b) The field of the branch Hamiltonian.** For each $t\in I_{0}$ the
function $H_{t}:=H(t,\cdot)$ is $C^{2}$ on $W$, and the **Hamiltonian field
of the presentation** at time $t$ is $X_{H_{t}}$:

$$X_{H_{t}}(x,p)=\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,\ -\nabla_{x}U(t,x)\bigr),$$

whose components are a velocity and a force. In the coordinates $X$ the
corresponding field is
$X_{\widetilde H_{t}}(q,P)=\bigl(G(q)^{-1}P,\ -\partial_{q}\widetilde H(t,q,P)\bigr)$,
where the second slot retains the kinetic contribution
$-\tfrac12P\cdot\partial_{q}(G(q)^{-1})P$ when the metric varies. If
$d\not\equiv0$ the model's forced evolution carries the additional momentum
source $d$; the corresponding vector field
$(x,p)\mapsto\bigl(\mathsf M^{-1}p,-\nabla_{x}U(t,x)+d(t,x,\mathsf M^{-1}p)\bigr)$
is generally not a Hamiltonian field for the presentation, and it is one
exactly when the residual force has a potential independent of the velocity
slot (the criterion is proved in clause 4 of the corresponding theorem of this
page).

**(c) Time dependence and status.** For a time-dependent $H$ the assignment
$t\mapsto X_{H_{t}}$ is a time-dependent field on the phase domain; each
$X_{H_{t}}$ is $C^{1}$, hence locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and no
completeness of its integral curves is asserted here. The item defines the
field datum and its chart expressions; the identification of the model's
motions with the integral curves, and all conservation or invariance
properties, are the subject of the other items of this page. The field is
defined by the intrinsic equation $\iota_{X}\omega=dH$ and therefore does not
depend on the canonical chart used to compute it.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the
momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]], the canonical
coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]] and the Hamiltonian fields of
[[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]]
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]). Let $W_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{2m_j}$ be
nonempty open subsets of phase domains of the presentation, carrying their
respective two-forms $\omega_j$ from [[def-cm13-two-form]] (for a
generalized-coordinate domain this is the pulled-back form $\omega_X$ in its
own $(q,P)$ coordinates). The dimensions $2m_1$ and $2m_2$ need not agree.

**(a) Pullback-preserving maps and transformations.** A $C^{1}$ map
$C:W_{1}\to W_{2}$ is a **canonical map of the presentation** when

$$C^{*}\omega_{2}=\omega_{1}\qquad\text{on }W_{1}$$

with pointwise pullback as in [[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]]. In
standard phase coordinates this is the dimension-aware matrix identity

$$DC(z)^{\mathsf T}J_{m_2}DC(z)=J_{m_1},$$

where $DC(z)$ is a $2m_2\times2m_1$ matrix and
$J_m=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_m\\-I_m&0\end{pmatrix}$. It forces $DC(z)$ to be
injective: if $DC(z)v=0$, then $v^{\mathsf T}J_{m_1}w=0$ for every $w$, so
$v=0$ by nondegeneracy of $J_{m_1}$, so $m_1\le m_2$. Thus it is a $C^1$
immersion preserving the symplectic forms (a symplectic immersion). If it is
also a $C^1$ embedding of the underlying
manifolds (injective and a homeomorphism onto its image), call it a
**canonical embedding**; pullback preservation alone asserts no global
injectivity or topological embedding.

When $m_1=m_2$, a canonical map is automatically a local diffeomorphism by
the inverse function theorem; call it a **local canonical transformation**.
A **canonical transformation** is a canonical map that is a $C^1$
diffeomorphism onto $W_2$. The same-dimensional definitions agree with the
finite-regularity convention of
[[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]]; the $C^\infty$ case agrees
with [[def-canonical-transformation]] and
[[def-symplectomorphism-local-symplectomorphism-and-symplectic-embedding]].
The different-dimensional definition here extends those finite-coordinate
notions only by the displayed pullback equality.

**(b) Equal-dimensional matrix and determinant tests.** If $m_1=m_2=m$,
then by [[prop-cm-canonical-map-tests-and-hamiltonian-transport]] clause 1
the pullback condition is equivalent to

$$DC(z)^{\mathsf T}J_m\,DC(z)=J_m\qquad\text{for every }z\in W_{1}.$$

The derivative is invertible at every point, so the map is a local
diffeomorphism by [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]. Taking
determinants of the matrix identity gives $(\det DC(z))^2=1$, hence
$|\det DC(z)|=1$ for every $z$
([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]],
[[cor-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-is-a-unit]],
[[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]). In dimension $2m\ge4$ the condition
$|\det DC|=1$ alone is strictly weaker than canonicity (the companion page
carries an explicit volume-preserving, non-canonical shear), while for $m=1$ the symplectic condition is exactly $\det DC=1$; absolute determinant $1$ alone also admits orientation-reversing, antisymplectic maps.
If $m_1\ne m_2$, $DC$ is rectangular, so no square determinant test is
defined; the dimension-aware pullback identity of clause (a) is the criterion.

**(c) Elementary closure and equal-dimensional field transport.** By
pointwise functoriality of pullback, the identity map, composites of
composable canonical maps and inverses of canonical transformations are
canonical. For a $C^{2}$ equal-dimensional canonical map
$C:W_{1}\to W_{2}$ and a $C^{2}$ function $f$ on $W_{2}$, the Hamiltonian
fields satisfy

$$DC(z)\,X_{f\circ C}(z)=X_{f}\bigl(C(z)\bigr)\qquad(z\in W_{1}),$$

so that $C$ conjugates the Hamiltonian system of $f\circ C$ to that of $f$
by the chain rule and the equal-dimensional matrix identity: taking the
inverse of $DC^{\mathsf T}J_mDC=J_m$ gives $DCJ_mDC^{\mathsf T}=J_m$, which
substituted into $DCJ_m\nabla(f\circ C)$ yields the displayed identity. No
such ambient field-transport identity is asserted for a lower-dimensional
symplectic immersion: the ambient field need not be tangent to its image.
Bracket, solution and phase-volume consequences are likewise limited to
their stated equal-dimensional local transformations.

**(d) The model's canonical maps.** For every generalized-coordinate
immersion $X$, the momentum map $\Phi_X$ in [[def-cm13-two-form]] is a
dimension-aware canonical map by clause 2 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]]; it is a symplectic immersion and is not
asserted to be a global embedding. When $r=3N$, its local branches and the
genuine transitions between such charts are equal-dimensional local
canonical transformations by clauses 2-3 of that theorem. The drift, kick and velocity-Verlet maps of the mechanical splitting in exact
arithmetic are equal-dimensional local canonical transformations on their
admissible domains whenever those domains are nonempty, by
[[prop-cm-drift-kick-and-verlet-preserve-the-canonical-form]].

**(e) Status.** The item defines the canonical maps of the presentation and
fixes the dimension-aware pullback test of clause (a) and the equal-dimensional
matrix test of clause (b). It asserts no existence of a canonical map beyond
the listed suppliers, no global statement on multiply connected phase domains
and no empirical content; in particular, canonicity is a local condition on
the two-form, and an equal-dimensional canonical transformation need not admit
a globally defined real generating function, as the scope remark of this page
records.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the
momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]], the canonical
coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]] and the Hamiltonian fields of
[[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]]. Dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]];
differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) Phase functions.** Let $W_{0}$ be a nonempty open subset of a phase
domain of the presentation. A **phase function of the presentation on
$W_{0}$ of class $C^{k}$** is a map $f:W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{k}$
($k\ge1$); its physical reading is a model quantity computed from the
positions and momenta of the labels, and its dimension is declared as part of
the datum. A **time-dependent phase function** on an interval $J\subseteq
I_{0}$ is a map $f:J\times W_{0}\to\mathbb R$ of the declared class, written
$f_{t}:=f(t,\cdot)$.

**(b) The bracket.** For $C^1$ phase functions $f,g:W_0\to\mathbb R$, define their **Poisson bracket for the presentation** by the pointwise coordinate formula $\{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g$ in a canonical chart, in the finite-regularity convention of [[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]]. This is a continuous function. The definition is independent of the canonical chart: for a canonical $C^1$ coordinate change with derivative $M$, the matrix identity implies $MJM^{\mathsf T}=J$, and the equivalence of the two matrix identities is proved in [[prop-cm-canonical-map-tests-and-hamiltonian-transport]], and the chain rule transforms the two gradients so their pairing is unchanged.

When both functions are $C^2$, their Hamiltonian fields of [[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]] are $C^1$, and the bracket has the intrinsic formula
$$\{f,g\}=\omega(X_f,X_g)=df(X_g)=X_g(f)=-X_f(g).$$
In this case it is $C^1$, with the same sign convention as the smooth root bracket and [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]. The extension to $C^1$ inputs makes evolution identities for $C^1$ observables and nested brackets of $C^2$ functions meaningful; it does not assert closure of the $C^2$ class under the bracket. Its dimension is $[f][g](\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1})^{-1}$, the product of the entries' dimensions divided by the action dimension of the two-form.

**(c) Coordinate formula.** In the Cartesian canonical coordinates $(x,p)$
of the presentation, and more generally in any canonical chart
$(\theta^{1},\dots,\theta^{2m})$ of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]],

$$\{f,g\}=\sum_{a=1}^{3N}\Bigl(f_{x^{a}}g_{p_{a}}-f_{p_{a}}g_{x^{a}}\Bigr)=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g,\qquad \{f,g\}=\sum_{a=1}^{m}\Bigl(f_{\theta^{a}}g_{\theta^{m+a}}-f_{\theta^{m+a}}g_{\theta^{a}}\Bigr),$$

with derivatives those of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. The coordinate formula is
recorded here and its identities (bilinearity, skew-symmetry, the Leibniz
rule, the Jacobi identity and the fundamental brackets) are proved in the
bracket-identities theorem of this page.

**(d) Status.** The item defines a bilinear operation on the declared phase
domain by the pointwise coordinate formula, and for $C^2$ entries by $\{f,g\}=\omega(X_f,X_g)$, hence
independently of the canonical chart used to evaluate the coordinate
formula. It asserts no equation of motion, no conservation law, no algebraic
identity beyond well-definedness and no measured value; in particular the
bracket with the Hamiltonian and the notion of first integral are the subject
of the evolution theorem of this page.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with standard two-form
$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]), and let
$H:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Write
$\nabla H=(H_{q^1},\dots,H_{q^n},H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n})$ for the Euclidean gradient
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and $J$ for the standard symplectic matrix. Then:

1. there is exactly one $C^1$ vector field $X_H$ on $U$ with $\iota_{X_H}\omega_U=dH$, and it is
   $$X_H=J\nabla H=\bigl(H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n},-H_{q^1},\dots,-H_{q^n}\bigr);$$
2. an integral curve $t\mapsto(q(t),p(t))$ of $X_H$ satisfies Hamilton's equations
   $$\dot q^i=H_{p_i}(q,p),\qquad \dot p_i=-H_{q^i}(q,p)\qquad(i=1,\dots,n);$$
3. for $f,g\in C^2(U)$ the Poisson bracket
   $\{f,g\}:=\omega_U(X_f,X_g)$ (in the finite-regularity convention of [[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]]) is
   $$\{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(f_{q^i}g_{p_i}-f_{p_i}g_{q^i}\bigr),$$
   hence $\{f,g\}=-\{g,f\}$, and $\{f,g\}$ is $C^1$ on $U$.

Let $n\ge1$. A **phase domain** is a nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Its points are written $z=(q,p)$ with
$q=(q^1,\dots,q^n)\in\mathbb R^n$ and $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\in\mathbb R^n$; the coordinate functions
$q^i,p_i:U\to\mathbb R$ are smooth ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and
$\partial_{q^1},\dots,\partial_{q^n},\partial_{p_1},\dots,\partial_{p_n}$ is the coordinate frame
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). On a phase domain:

1. the **canonical one-form** is the smooth one-form
   $\lambda_U:=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\,dq^i\in\Omega^1(U)$;
2. the **standard symplectic two-form** is the smooth two-form
   $\omega_U:=\sum_{i=1}^n dq^i\wedge dp_i\in\Omega^2(U)$
   ([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]);
3. the **standard symplectic matrix** is the block matrix
   $$J:=\begin{pmatrix}0_n&I_n\\-I_n&0_n\end{pmatrix}\in M_{2n}(\mathbb R),$$
   whose blocks are $n\times n$.

The identity $\omega_U=-d\lambda_U$ holds, because the coordinate formula for the exterior
derivative ([[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]]) gives
$d\lambda_U=\sum_i dp_i\wedge dq^i=-\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$. When $U$ is an induced chart domain of a
cotangent bundle, the published [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]] identifies
$\lambda_U$ and $\omega_U$ with the tautological one-form and the canonical cotangent two-form in
those coordinates; the present definition is the choice-free local coordinate model that the
canonical-calculus items of this page use.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be continuous on an open time-state-parameter domain and locally state-Lipschitz with one constant on compact cylinders. Near fixed data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$, the solutions supplied by Picard-Lindelof exist on one common compact time interval and depend jointly and uniformly continuously there on the initial time, initial state, and parameter. Quantitatively, if the common time interval has length at most $H$, $\|F\|_2\le M$, and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$, then solutions through $(t_0,x_0)$ and $(s,y_0)$ satisfy

$$\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2\le e^{LH}\bigl(\|x_0-y_0\|_2+M|s-t_0|+H\,\omega(\|\lambda-\mu\|_2)\bigr),$$

where $\omega(r)\to0$ is a uniform modulus for the parameter dependence of $F$ on that cylinder.

Let $F:D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and
$C^1$ in the state variable. Fix data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$ and a compact time
interval $I=[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ on which the corresponding solutions through nearby
initial states all exist. Then the solution map

$$\Phi:I\times U_0\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad \Phi(t,y)=x(t;y),$$

is $C^1$ in the initial-state variable $y$ on some neighbourhood $U_0$ of
$x_0$. For each $y\in U_0$, the derivative matrix
$D_y\Phi(t,y)$ is the solution of the variational equation along $t\mapsto x(t;y)$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let
$F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the state variable, let
$x:J\to\mathbb R^n$ be a solution of

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

on an interval $J$, and let $t_0\in J$. The **variational equation along $x$**
is the linear matrix ODE

$$A'(t)=D_xF(t,x(t))\,A(t),\qquad A(t_0)=I_n,$$

where $D_xF(t,x(t))$ is the Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives of the state
variables, read via [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] from the
$C^1$ regularity recorded in [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]].
Its solutions are matrix-valued curves $A:J\to M_n(\mathbb R)$.

For an autonomous equation $x'=V(x)$ with $V$ of class $C^1$, this becomes

$$A'(t)=DV(x(t))\,A(t),\qquad A(t_0)=I_n.$$

It is the linearized equation governing first-order variation of nearby
solutions with respect to their initial data.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.
For a $C^2$ scalar field $f$, $H_f(a)^T=H_f(a)$ at every point $a$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the **transpose** of $A$ is the matrix
$A^{\mathsf T}\in M_{n\times m}(F)$ defined by

$$(A^{\mathsf T})_{ji}:=a_{ij}.$$

Thus transposition interchanges rows and columns. The transpose of a zero-sized
matrix is the unique matrix of the transposed zero-sized shape.

A matrix $A\in M_n(F)$ is **invertible** when there is a matrix $B\in M_n(F)$
such that

$$AB=I_n=BA.$$

Such a $B$ is unique and is denoted $A^{-1}$. The **general linear set** is

$$\operatorname{GL}_n(F):=\{A\in M_n(F):A\text{ is invertible}\}.$$

It is the set of units of the ring $M_n(F)$. The fact that it is a group under
matrix multiplication is [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]. For $n=0$,
the unique empty matrix is $I_0$ and is its own inverse.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $n\geq1$, and $A\in M_n(R)$. Then $A$ is
invertible if and only if $\det(A)$ is a unit of $R$.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

For every $n\ge1$, every commutative ring $R$, and every $A\in M_n(R)$,
$$\det(A^{\mathsf T})=\det(A).$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

derivations.claim: By [F2] the right-hand side $F(t,z)=J\nabla H(t,z)$ is continuous and $C^{1}$ in the state variable, and for the given base data there are $h>0$ and a neighbourhood $U_{0}$ on which the solution map $\Phi$ is defined and $C^{1}$ in $y$, with $Y(t):=D_{y}\Phi(t;y)$ solving $Y'=J\,\mathrm{Hess}\,H(t,\Phi(t;y))\,Y$ and $Y(t_{0})=I$.

Along that solution, $\frac{d}{dt}(Y^{\mathsf T}J\,Y)=Y'^{\mathsf T}J\,Y+Y^{\mathsf T}J\,Y'=Y^{\mathsf T}\mathrm{Hess}\,H(t,\Phi)\,J^{\mathsf T}J\,Y+Y^{\mathsf T}J\,J\,\mathrm{Hess}\,H(t,\Phi)\,Y$; since $J^{\mathsf T}J=-J^{2}=I$ and $\mathrm{Hess}\,H$ is symmetric [F3], the two terms cancel, so $t\mapsto Y(t)^{\mathsf T}J\,Y(t)$ has vanishing derivative on the interval and equals $I^{\mathsf T}JI=J$ at $t_{0}$; by [F3] each entry is constant, so $Y(t)^{\mathsf T}J\,Y(t)=J$ for every $t\in[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]$.

From $Y^{\mathsf T}J\,Y=J$ with $J$ invertible, $Y$ is invertible ($Yv=0$ implies $Jv=Y^{\mathsf T}JYv=0$, hence $v=0$) and taking inverses gives $Y^{-1}J^{-1}Y^{-T}=J^{-1}$, that is $Y^{-1}J\,Y^{-T}=J$ in view of $J^{-1}=-J$; multiplying on the left by $Y$ and on the right by $Y^{\mathsf T}$ gives $YJ\,Y^{\mathsf T}=J$. Moreover $\det Y(t)=1$: the identity $Y^{\mathsf T}JY=J$ gives $(\det Y)^{2}\det J=\det J$, so $\det Y(t)=\pm1$, and $t\mapsto\det Y(t)$ is continuous with $\det Y(t_{0})=1$, so the determinant is $+1$ throughout.

Clause 1: by step 2.1 the derivative of the time-$t$ map satisfies the matrix identity at every $y\in U_{0}$, so by the canonicity criterion of [F1] the map $\Phi_{t}$ is canonical and $\Phi_{t}^{*}\omega=\omega$; by step 3.1, $\det D\Phi_{t}=1$.

Clause 2: since $f,g$ are $C^2$ and $\Phi_t$ is $C^1$, both $f\circ\Phi_t$ and $g\circ\Phi_t$ are $C^1$. Their brackets are therefore defined by the pointwise $C^1$ coordinate extension of [[def-cm13-poisson]]. The chain rule [F3] gives $
abla(f\circ\Phi_t)=D\Phi_t^{\mathsf T}(
abla f)\circ\Phi_t$ and similarly for $g$, so the coordinate formula gives $\{f\circ\Phi_t,g\circ\Phi_t\}=(
abla f\circ\Phi_t)^{\mathsf T}D\Phi_tJ D\Phi_t^{\mathsf T}(
abla g\circ\Phi_t)=(
abla f\circ\Phi_t)^{\mathsf T}J(
abla g\circ\Phi_t)=\{f,g\}\circ\Phi_t$, using $D\Phi_tJ D\Phi_t^{\mathsf T}=J$ from step 3.1 and [F1].

Clause 3: on the potential branch the curves $t\mapsto\Phi(t;y)$ solve the Hamiltonian system, hence are, by [[pthm-cm13-hamiltonian-field-integrates-the-model-equations]] clause 1, the momentum-phase curves of the model's motions; the canonicity, bracket preservation and unit determinant of clauses 1-2 are local-in-time statements on the actual time-slice domains, and no completeness is asserted.
Collection: clause 1 is step 4.1, clause 2 is step 4.2 and clause 3 is step 5.1; this proves the statement.

boundaries.reason: The base point z0 and t0 are supplied, and step 1.1 obtains an open neighbourhood of that point and a positive time radius.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 has Y(t0)=I, and step 2.1 establishes zero derivative of Y-transpose*J*Y. This zero is an exact invariant derivative; the flow at the initial time is identity, and no zero Jacobian is permitted by step 3.1.
At N=1 the variational matrix in step 1.1 has six rows and the canonical identity in step 2.1 is unchanged; there is no assumption of multiple particle labels.
The degenerate cases are those excluded by the hypotheses: the solution map is a local diffeomorphism with invertible derivative, so no singular map is claimed (step 1.1).

The conclusion is asserted on the closed time interval $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ including its endpoints (statement); the determinant clause of step 3.1 uses continuity from $t_0$, so the endpoint values are included.

boundaries.reason: Step 1.1 applies the unique-IVP dependence supplier at one datum; the solution map is unique and step 2.1 differentiates it, rather than selecting solutions separately.
Statement proves local canonicity, bracket preservation and unit determinant of the specified flow; it supplies no converse characterization of arbitrary canonical maps as flows.
