citations.quote:
Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing
regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
generalized-coordinate map with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$,
kinetic metric $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$ and substituted
potential $\widetilde U(t,q)=U(t,X(q))$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]), and let $H$ and
$\widetilde H$ be the Hamiltonians of [[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]. Then:

1. **(Cartesian chart)** The fibre momentum map
   $\mathbb F_{t,x}(v)=\mathsf Mv$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ onto
   $\mathbb R^{3N}$ for every $(t,x)\in I_{0}\times Q$, and the inverse
   Legendre branch is the $C^{2}$ map
   $v(t,x,p)=\mathsf M^{-1}p$ on the whole phase chart
   $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$. Hence the presentation is
   hyperregular on the Cartesian chart in the sense of
   [[def-cm12-hyperregularity]], and the Hamiltonian of the branch is

$$H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x),$$

with the dot product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]],

   a $C^{2}$ function of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.

2. **(generalized-coordinate chart)** The fibre map
   $v\mapsto G(q)v$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R^{r}$ onto $\mathbb R^{r}$
   for every $(t,q)\in I_{0}\times\Omega$, and the inverse Legendre branch is
   the $C^{2}$ map $v(t,q,p)=G(q)^{-1}p$ on
   $I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$. Hence the presentation is
   hyperregular on the chart of $X$, and the Hamiltonian in the coordinates
   $X$ is

$$\widetilde H(t,q,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot G(q)^{-1}p+\widetilde U(t,q),$$

   a $C^{2}$ function of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch and the declared
presentation; it asserts no equation of motion, no conservation law and no
empirical content.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential $U$ and residual forces $d$ of
the standing regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]); dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]] and the Euclidean pairing is
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

**(a) Cartesian Hamiltonian.** Assume the presentation is hyperregular on the
Cartesian chart, with inverse Legendre branch
$v:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-cm12-hyperregularity]], [[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]]).
The **Hamiltonian of the presentation on the Cartesian chart** is the function

$$H:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad H(t,x,p):=p\cdot v(t,x,p)-L\bigl(t,x,v(t,x,p)\bigr),$$

where $p\cdot v(t,x,p)$ is the Euclidean pairing of the momentum covector
with the inverse-branch velocity ([[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). The momentum phase chart
$I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with coordinates $(t,x,p)$ is the
**Hamiltonian phase chart** of the presentation on the Cartesian chart.
If $Q=\varnothing$, the formula denotes the unique empty function; the
identification with the cited mathematical fibre-full chart applies only
when $Q\ne\varnothing$.

**(b) Generalized-coordinate Hamiltonian.** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
generalized-coordinate map with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$, kinetic
metric $G$ and inverse Legendre branch $v$ on
$I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ ([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]). The **Hamiltonian of the presentation in the
coordinates $X$** is

$$\widetilde H:I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad \widetilde H(t,q,p):=p\cdot v(t,q,p)-\widetilde L\bigl(t,q,v(t,q,p)\bigr).$$

For the Cartesian chart when $Q\ne\varnothing$, $X=\mathrm{id}$ and
$\widetilde H=H$; the general
definition is the same formula applied to the substituted fibre-full chart.

**(c) Dimensions and conventions.** Each term of the defining difference has
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (energy): the pairing $p\cdot v$ multiplies
$\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ by $\ell\tau^{-1}$ in Cartesian data
([[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]), and $L$ has energy dimension
([[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]]). In the coordinates $X$ the
pairing is dimensionally consistent for every declared coordinate dimension
$\gamma_{a}$ and the dimension is unchanged. The Hamiltonian is $C^{1}$ on
its domain, being a sum of products of $C^{1}$ maps
([[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]],
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). The pairing is the coordinate
Euclidean product; no metric on momentum space and no symplectic form is
introduced by this definition.

**(d) Dependence and status.** The Hamiltonian depends on the declared chart,
on its inverse Legendre branch, uniquely determined on that chart by fibre
bijectivity ([[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]), and on the potential
representative: replacing $U$ by $U+c(t)$ leaves the branch unchanged and
replaces $L$ by $L-c(t)$, hence replaces $H$ by $H+c(t)$
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause (c),
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] clause (b)). It asserts no
equation of motion, no conservation property and no measured value; the
explicit kinetic-plus-potential form of $H$ for the mechanical branch, the
equivalence of its equations with the model's equation of motion and its
relation to the mechanical energy are the theorems of this page. Matrix
identities used by those theorems are read through
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]].

Adopt the force model and one inertial frame of
[[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]], with configuration domain $Q$, time
window $I_{0}$ and force map $F$. Dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]]
and gradients are Euclidean ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]); points of
$Q$ are written $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$ with $x_{i}\in\mathbb R^{3}$.

**(a) Potential representation of the force map.** A model **presents its
force map through a potential** when it declares a function
$$U:I_{0}\times Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$
of class $C^{2}$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), of
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules), with
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N)$$
for every $(t,x,v)$ of the state domain; here $\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ is the
gradient of $u\mapsto U(t,x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1},u,x_{i+1},\dots,x_{N})$ at
$u=x_{i}$. More generally, a model may declare **residual forces**
$d_{i}:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of the standing
regularity of clause (iii) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and present
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)+d_{i}(t,x,v);$$
the pair $(U,d)$ is then the model's presentation and
$F_{i}^{\mathrm{p}}:=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ is its **potential part**. The scalar
$U$ is a **potential energy** for the model's potential part; the framework's
earlier admission of potentials in [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (iii) is
the special case $d\equiv0$. A model that presents its whole force map this
way with $d\equiv0$ is a **global potential model** (the term "conservative
model" is used only in this sense).

**(b) Potential and mechanical energy along a curve family.** For a curve
family $x:J\to Q$ of the model ([[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]]
clause (a)) define the **potential energy along the family** and the
**mechanical energy** by
$$U_{x}(t):=U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad E(t):=K(t)+U_{x}(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
with $K$ the kinetic energy of the definition. The potential part contributes
to the force field but not directly to $K$; $E$ is defined only along the
potential branch of the model, and along a motion it is the subject of the
energy balance of this page.

**(c) Normalization of the potential.** Let $c:I_0\to\mathbb R$ be
differentiable and put $\widetilde U:=U+c(t)$, retaining $C^2$ regularity
when a potential presentation of the standing class is required. The spatial
gradient is unchanged, so this presents the same potential part with the same
residual forces. The full converse is componentwise: if $\widetilde U$ and
$U$ are $C^2$ and have the same spatial gradient, then on each connected
component $C$ of the open set $Q$ there is a $C^2$ function
$c_C:I_0\to\mathbb R$ with
$$\widetilde U(t,x)-U(t,x)=c_C(t)\qquad(x\in C).$$
Here a connected component is a maximal connected subset of $Q$. For fixed
$t$, the difference is constant on every ball contained in $Q$: along any
segment in the ball its derivative is the vanishing spatial gradient paired
with the segment direction. The difference is consequently locally constant,
and on a connected component it is constant, since a value's level set and
its complement are both relatively open. Evaluating at any fixed point of
$C$ gives the $C^2$ regularity of $c_C$. Conversely, independent such functions
on the components give a $C^2$ potential with unchanged spatial gradient;
components of an open Euclidean set are open, because each sufficiently small
ball about one of their points is connected and lies in that component.
A single $c(t)$ describes every ambiguity precisely when the component
functions agree, in particular when $Q$ is connected. No agreement follows
from openness alone: on two disjoint balls the potentials $0$ and the function
equal to $0$ on one ball and $1$ on the other have the same force. Every
continuous motion on an interval remains in one component, so its energy
shifts by that component's $c_C(t)$ and its energy rate by $c_C'(t)$.
The representative is part of the model's declaration, and every energy
statement names it.

**(d) Closed and exact force fields.** A **time- and velocity-independent
configuration-space force field** is a $C^{1}$ map
$\varphi=(\varphi_{1},\dots,\varphi_{N}):Q\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$, where
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is the open configuration domain and each
$\varphi_i(x)$ is the force on label $i$ at configuration $x$; its components
have force dimension. It represents a force map of the form
$F_i(t,x,v)=\varphi_i(x)$ on the model's state domain. This configuration-space
field is not in general an external single-label force: to identify its
$i$th component with an external map of [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (i),
one must further require that it depend on $x_i$ alone, as in the declared
signature $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}(t,x_i,v_i)$. Such a field is **closed** when
$\partial_{k}\varphi_{j}=\partial_{j}\varphi_{k}$ for all coordinate indices
$j,k\in\{0,\dots,3N-1\}$ at every point of $Q$, using the flattened
coordinate indices of [[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]], and **exact with potential
energy $U$** when $\varphi=-\nabla U$ for a $C^{2}$ function
$U:Q\to\mathbb R$; equivalently, the field $-\varphi$ is exact in the sense
of [[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]] with potential $U$. The following
mathematical facts are used, with their proofs at the cited items:

1. every exact field is closed, by equality of mixed partial derivatives
   ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], applied to the $C^2$ potential);
2. on a star-shaped open domain every closed $C^{1}$ field is exact, by the
   Poincaré lemma ([[thm-poincare-lemma-for-star-shaped-domains]]);
3. beyond item 2 this item asserts **no** implication from closedness to
   global exactness: on a general open domain a closed field need not have a
   potential energy, and the criterion used by the framework is exactness as
   defined above.

Consequently the existence of a global potential energy on the model's
configuration domain is a property of the field on that domain, and a model
whose potential part is a merely closed field on a non-star-shaped domain is
not thereby a global potential model. The distinction is sharp: the
companion examples page carries a model on an annular domain whose force
field is smooth and closed, has nonzero circulation around a closed loop, and
therefore admits no global potential and no global conserved energy of the
form $K+U$, while item 2 provides a local potential and a locally conserved
energy on every star-shaped subpart of that domain.

**(e) Local potentials.** Let $V\subseteq Q$ be open and star-shaped with
respect to one of its points ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]) and let
$\varphi$ be closed on $V$. Then item 2 of (d) provides a $C^{2}$ potential
$U_{V}:V\to\mathbb R$ with $\varphi|_{V}=-\nabla U_{V}$: a **local potential**
of the field on $V$. On the restricted configuration domain $V$ the model
with force $-\nabla U_{V}$ is a global potential model, so the mechanical
energy $K+U_{V}$ is available along curve families in $V$; this is how a
potential is recovered from a merely closed field on a sufficiently small
star-shaped piece of the domain, with no claim of a global representative.

**(f) Equipotential level sets.** For this clause assume additionally that
$U:Q\to\mathbb R$ is smooth, meaning $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); the potential presentations
of clause (a) still require only $C^2$. Let
$c\in\mathbb R$ and suppose $U^{-1}(c)\neq\varnothing$ and $\nabla
U(x)\neq0$ for every $x\in U^{-1}(c)$; equivalently $c$ is a regular value of
$U$ and every point of the level set is a regular point
([[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]]). Then $U^{-1}(c)$ is an
embedded submanifold of $Q$ of dimension $3N-1$
([[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]],
[[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]). No such conclusion is made at a
level where $\nabla U$ vanishes somewhere on the level set, where the level
set may have singular points.

**(g) Status.** The potential, its normalization, the residual forces and the
declaration of a potential presentation are model data; the closed/exact
statements of (d)-(f) are cited mathematics about the declared field. This
item asserts no conservation law, no force law of nature and no measured
value.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about
forces and motion, in the spacetime, frames and worldlines of
[[post-cm01-spacetime]], [[post-cm01-frames]] and [[post-cm01-worldlines]].

**(i) Setting and configuration domain.** A model of the framework has
$N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed positive masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]], clause (v)) and a configuration domain $Q$ in one
fixed inertial frame, in the unconstrained branch of
[[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a): $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open,
possibly with the collision set $\Delta$ removed when the force law of the
model is singular at coincident positions. The constrained branch of that
definition, with its reaction forces, is **not** covered by this postulate; the
dynamics of constrained systems is a separate development with its own
assumptions. A **state** of the model is a pair $z=(x,v)\in Q\times\mathbb
R^{3N}$ of positions and coordinate velocities of the labels in the chosen
frame ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]).

**(ii) Time window.** A model carries a nondegenerate open interval
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, its **time window**, read in seconds
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(iii) Force map and standing regularity.** A **force map** on this data is a
map

$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v)=\bigl(F_{1}(t,x,v),\dots,F_{N}(t,x,v)\bigr),$$

with components of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
([[def-cm01-units]]). The standing hypotheses of this branch, which every
force map of a model is required to satisfy, are:

1. **Continuity.** $F$ is continuous on its domain
   $D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
2. **State-local Lipschitz regularity, locally uniform in time.** $F$ is
   locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z=(x,v)$, locally uniformly in
   time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]: every
   compact cylinder $C\subseteq D$ carries a finite $L\ge0$ with
   $\lVert F(t,z)-F(t,z')\rVert_{2}\le L\lVert z-z'\rVert_{2}$ whenever
   $(t,z),(t,z')\in C$ share their time coordinate.

A map that fails clause 1 or clause 2 is **not** a force map of this branch,
whatever its other merits. When a later statement differentiates the force map
(for instance in a linearization or a smooth-dependence claim), it adds the
required differentiability hypothesis of the state variable explicitly; clause
2 alone licenses only the existence, uniqueness and continuation statements
proved on this page.

**(iv) Equation of motion.** Adopt: the motion of the labels of a model with
force map $F$ in an inertial frame is governed by

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N),$$

imposed along families of $C^{2}$ coordinate curves of the labels
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):J\to Q$, where $J\subseteq I_{0}$ is an interval with
nonempty interior and the derivatives are those of
[[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. The precise notion of a motion of the
model, its associated first-order system and its maximal motions is
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. The force map is **primitive data** of the model:
the equations above are the model's law, not an operational definition of $F$
from a measured acceleration, and $F$ is not an extra observable measured
independently of the motion. The mass $m_{i}$ in (iv) is the fixed inertial
mass of clause (v) of [[post-cm01-worldlines]]; no other mass occurs in this
clause.

**(v) Additive composition of force contributions.** When a model presents its
force map as composed of contributions, the composition is the pointwise sum:
for force maps $F^{(1)},\dots,F^{(k)}$ on a common domain satisfying (iii),

$$F(t,z)=\sum_{a=1}^{k}F^{(a)}(t,z),$$

and the sum again satisfies (iii), because a finite sum of continuous maps is
continuous and a finite sum of maps that are locally Lipschitz in the state
variable is locally Lipschitz with a locally uniform constant. This
**superposition of forces** is an adopted modelling rule, not a theorem about
nature: it says how the model's total force is composed from the contributions
it declares. Two decompositions with the same sum define the same force map
and the same model; the framework does not measure an individual contribution
in isolation, and no observation of motions alone determines a decomposition.
Nor does (v) assert that sums of motions are motions: if $F$ is not affine in
the state, the sum of two solutions of (iv) generally does not satisfy (iv),
and superposing solutions is a separate question from superposing forces.

**(vi) Description in another inertial frame.** Let $F_{*}=\bigl(o',u',
(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}')\bigr)$ be a second inertial frame related to the frame
of (i) by the Galilean transformation

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x_i'=Rx_i+\upsilon t+a_{0}\quad(i=1,\dots,N)$$

with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a_{0},\upsilon\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in SO(3)$
([[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]] clause 1;
[[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]); $\upsilon$ is the boost velocity
denoted by $v$ in that theorem. Define the block-diagonal map
$$R_{N}:=\operatorname{diag}(R,\dots,R):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$$
and the repeated tuples $\bar a_{0}:=(a_{0},\dots,a_{0})$ and
$\bar\upsilon:=(\upsilon,\dots,\upsilon)$ in $(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$. Thus
$R_N x=(Rx_{1},\dots,Rx_{N})$, and the same componentwise rule applies to
velocities and forces; since $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3}$,
$R_N^{\mathsf T}R_N=I_{3N}$. If $x:J\to Q$ is a family of motions of the
labels in the first frame, then the description of the same worldlines in the second
frame is
$$\eta(t'):=R_{N}x(t'-b)+\bar\upsilon(t'-b)+\bar a_{0}\qquad(t'\in J+b).$$
By clause 2 of the cited theorem, each $\eta_i$ is $C^{2}$ and
$\eta_i''(t')=R\ddot x_i(t'-b)$, so along the motion
$$m_i\eta_i''(t')=R F_i\bigl(t'-b,x(t'-b),\dot x(t'-b)\bigr).$$

Adopt: the same interaction, read in the second frame, is represented on the
transferred data by the force map below. Let $P$ be the inverse affine
transfer from new-frame data to old-frame data,
$$P(t',y,w):=\bigl(t'-b,\,R_N^{\mathsf T}(y-\bar\upsilon(t'-b)-\bar a_{0}),\,R_N^{\mathsf T}(w-\bar\upsilon)\bigr).$$
Its preimage of the original domain is
$$D_{*}:=P^{-1}(D)=\{(t',y,w):P(t',y,w)\in D\};$$
it is open because $P$ is a homeomorphism and $D$ is open. Define
$$F_{*}:D_{*}\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad F_{*}(t',y,w):=R_N F\Bigl(t'-b,\ R_N^{\mathsf T}\bigl(y-\bar\upsilon(t'-b)-\bar a_{0}\bigr),\ R_N^{\mathsf T}(w-\bar\upsilon)\Bigr).$$
The map $F_{*}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in its state variable:
the transfer and its inverse are affine, and at fixed time they act linearly
on state differences; on compact time intervals their state Lipschitz
constants are uniform, so precomposition preserves the stated regularity of
$F$. The framework
formulates the equation of motion in every inertial frame; a rule that does
not transform by this law is a description tied to the frame in which it was
written, and the framework attaches no kinematic covariance to it. When
$Q=\mathbb R^{3N}$ — the case of the models of the companion page — the
transferred domain is again a product
$I_{0}'\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with $I_{0}'=I_{0}+b$, and
$F_{*}$ is a force map in the sense of (iii); for a proper open $Q$ the
transferred position set $R_NQ+\bar\upsilon(t'-b)+\bar a_0$ may depend on
$t'$, and the equation is then read on that transferred set.

**(vii) What this branch excludes.** Impulsive forcing (a finite momentum
transfer at an instant is not a force map); Coulomb sliding friction, whose
expression contains the factor $v/\lvert v\rvert$ and is undefined at $v=0$;
static friction, which requires an inequality or a set-valued reaction model;
stochastic forcing; and forces that exist only as distributions. Each of these
requires its own stated model and solution notion, and none is covered by
(iii)–(iv). A singular force law is admissible on a configuration domain with
the singular configurations removed — for instance an inverse-square law on
the collision-excluded $Q$ of clause (i) — and what the removal of those
configurations implies for existence in time is stated by the continuation
theorem of this page.

**(viii) Status.** Clause (iii) states the hypotheses under which the theorems
of this page are proved; clause (iv) is the adopted law of motion; clauses (v)
and (vi) are the adopted composition and frame rules. Nothing here is deduced
from experiment, from a symmetry principle or from the uniqueness theory of
differential equations, and nothing here asserts that any physical
interaction is exactly of this form: the theorems of this page are conditional
consequences of the adopted model. The empirical significance of a concrete
model lies in fully specified model parameters and reported observations
compared with its predictions, and this postulate supplies neither.

Let $N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ be given as
in [[post-cm01-worldlines]], and fix one inertial frame of the model with
spatial coordinates $x_{i}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ for each label $i$. Identify the
space of all position tuples with $\mathbb R^{3N}=(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ and
write its points as $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$; each component $x_{i}$ has
dimension $\ell$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(a) Unconstrained branch.** The **unconstrained configuration domain** is an
open set $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, chosen as part of the model. A tuple
$x\in Q$ is an **admissible configuration**: an assignment of one position to
each label at one time. A **singular-force exclusion** is the removal of the
**collision set**

$$\Delta:=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:\ \text{there are }i\ne j\text{ with }x_{i}=x_{j}\Bigr\}$$

from the domain, which is done when the model's force law is not defined at
coincident positions: $\Delta$ is closed (it is the union of the finitely many
closed sets $\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}$, each the zero set of the continuous map
$x\mapsto x_{i}-x_{j}$), so $Q:=\mathbb R^{3N}\setminus\Delta$ is open and is a
legitimate configuration domain. Whether the exclusion is part of the model is
a modelling decision recorded with the force law; the framework itself only
requires $Q$ to be open and stated.

**(b) Holonomic constraint branch.** Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ be an open
**ambient set**, let $k\in\mathbb N$ with $1\le k\le3N-1$, and let

$$G=(G_{1},\dots,G_{k}):O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k}$$

be a smooth map, each component carrying a declared dimension and unit fixed
by the model (a component can always be rescaled by a nonzero constant without
changing its zero set, and the rescaling is part of the declaration). Assume:

1. **Nonempty level set:** $G^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing$;
2. **Rank condition:** the differential $DG(x):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k}$
   is surjective, equivalently has rank $k$, at every $x\in G^{-1}(0)$.

Then $0$ is a regular value of $G$ in the sense of
[[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]], and the **constrained
configuration space** is $Q:=G^{-1}(0)$. By
[[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] — applied to the smooth
map $G$ from the open subset $O$ of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ to $\mathbb R^{k}$, whose
regular value $0$ has nonempty fibre — $Q$ is an embedded submanifold of
$\mathbb R^{3N}$ of dimension $3N-k$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]).
The **degrees of freedom** of this branch of the model is the number
$$\dim Q=3N-k.$$ In the sense of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]], $Q$ together with the inclusion $X:Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$ is then a particle configuration, and the mass metric of that definition is available with the masses $m_{i}$; the configuration is constrained to $Q$ for all times in this branch.

**(c) Time-dependent holonomic constraints.** If the constraint map depends on
time,

$$G:\mathbb R\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k},\qquad (t,x)\longmapsto G(t,x),$$

with $G$ smooth and $D_{x}G(t_{0},x)$ of rank $k$ at every $x$ of the nonempty
set $G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$, then for each fixed $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$ the
**instantaneous configuration space** $Q_{t_{0}}:=G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$ is an
embedded submanifold of dimension $3N-k$ by the same theorem applied to
$G(t_{0},\cdot)$. The family $\{Q_{t_{0}}\}$ varies with $t_{0}$; a curve
$t\mapsto q(t)$ with $G(t,q(t))=0$ is not thereby a curve in one fixed
manifold, and the kinematic treatment of such constraints (velocities, the
reaction forces that maintain them and the distinction between rheonomic and
scleronomic constraints) belongs to the framework's constraint development and
is not part of this definition.

**(d) Mass operator.** In the ambient coordinates define the **mass operator**
$\mathsf M:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ by block multiplication,

$$\mathsf M(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):=(m_{1}x_{1},\dots,m_{N}x_{N});$$

its matrix in the standard basis is block diagonal with blocks $m_{i}I_{3}$,
the **mass matrix** of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]].
Its dimension is $\mu$: it multiplies positions of dimension $\ell$ by masses
of dimension $\mu$. On the constrained branch, for the inclusion
$X:Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$ and tangent vectors $h,z\in T_qQ$,
the mass metric of that item is
$$\mathcal G_q(h,z):=\langle dX_q(h),\mathsf M\,dX_q(z)\rangle_{3N}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}m_i\,h_i\cdot z_i,$$
where $h_i,z_i\in\mathbb R^3$ are the blocks of $dX_q(h),dX_q(z)$ under
the canonical Euclidean tangent identification specified in that supplier.
It restricts the mass-weighted ambient bilinear form to $T_qQ$, rather than
the unweighted Euclidean inner product.

**(e) Velocity constraints are a different object.** A **velocity-map
constraint** on the open ambient set $O$ is a pair of smooth maps
$$A:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'\times3N},\qquad b:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'},\qquad 1\le k'\le3N,$$
with $A(t,x)$ of constant rank $k'$ everywhere in the declared domain,
imposing $A(t,x(t))\dot x(t)+b(t,x(t))=0$ on a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to O$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval, the parameter $t$ is frame time, and $\dot x(t):=x'(t)$ is the componentwise derivative in the convention of [[def-cm01-units]]. Equivalently $A(t,x)$ is a linear map
$\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k'}$. Each row's output unit is declared, and
its corresponding component of $b$ has that same unit. The allowed velocities
at $(t,x)$ form the affine set $\{v:A(t,x)v+b(t,x)=0\}$; its differences form
$\ker A(t,x)$.

The law is **locally holonomic-equivalent at $(t_0,x_0)$** if on some open
neighbourhood $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times O$ of that point there are a $C^2$
map $g:V\to\mathbb R^{k'}$ with $D_xg$ of rank $k'$ and a $C^2$ matrix map
$C:V\to\mathbb R^{k'\times k'}$ with $\det C\ne0$ such that
$$A=C\,D_xg,\qquad b=C\,\partial_tg\qquad\text{on }V.$$
Thus the velocity law is locally the derivative of the regular positional
constraints $g(t,x)=\text{constant}$. It is **locally nonholonomic at the
specified point** when no such neighbourhood and pair $(g,C)$ exists; a
nonholonomic model in this local sense declares a point (or a region of
points) with this failure. For a homogeneous time-independent law this
rules out such a regular-level-set representation throughout a neighbourhood.
It need not rule out an individual embedded submanifold $S\subseteq O$ with
$T_xS=\ker A(x)$ for every $x\in S$, using the ambient tangent identification
of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]]; for an affine
time-dependent law the criterion also includes the drift $b$.
Absence of a single global pair alone does not establish local
nonintegrability. The rank of $A$ counts instantaneous velocity restrictions,
not the dimension of a positional configuration manifold; accessibility
requires its own definition. Rank changes require a separate model.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $(t,z(t))\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $(t,z(t))\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]], the canonical
coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]], the Hamiltonian fields of
[[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]], the canonical maps of
[[def-cm13-canonical-map]] and the branch Hamiltonian $H$ of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]] and [[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]]
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], [[def-cm01-configuration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). Write $n':=3N$. Let $O_q,O_Q\subseteq Q$ be nonempty open
Cartesian position-coordinate sets, and let $O_P\subseteq\mathbb R^{n'}$
be a nonempty open momentum-coordinate set. In clause 2 require
$S_P(q,P)\in O_Q$ for every $(q,P)\in O_q\times O_P$; only
local branches with source in $O_q\times\mathbb R^{n'}$ and target in
$O_Q\times\mathbb R^{n'}$ are called maps of the presentation. Then:

1. **(first kind)** Let $S:O_{q}\times O_{Q}\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^{3}$
   with $\det S_{qQ}(q,Q)\neq0$ everywhere
   ([[def-cm-generating-function-of-the-first-and-second-kind]]), and define
   the **local map generated by $S$** by solving $p=S_{q}(q,Q)$ for
   $Q=Q(q,p)$ and setting $P:=-S_{Q}(q,Q)$: a $C^{2}$ map
   $C:(q,p)\mapsto(Q,P)$ defined on a neighbourhood of each point of the
   solution set. Then $C$ is a canonical $C^{2}$ local diffeomorphism of the
   presentation: $DC^{\mathsf T}J\,DC=J$, $C^{*}\omega=\omega$ and
   $|\det DC|=1$; and the one-form identity $p\cdot dq-P\cdot dQ=dS$ holds on
   the $(q,Q)$-domain ([[prop-cm-generating-functions-yield-canonical-maps]]).
2. **(second kind)** Let $S:O_{q}\times O_{P}\to\mathbb R$ be $C^{3}$ with
   $\det S_{qP}\neq0$ everywhere, and define the local map by
   $p=S_{q}(q,P)$, $Q=S_{P}(q,P)$. Then it is again a canonical $C^{2}$ local
   diffeomorphism of the presentation with the recorded identity
   $p\cdot dq+Q\cdot dP=dS$.
3. **(local converse)** Let $C$ be a $C^{2}$ canonical diffeomorphism between
   nonempty open subsets of the presentation's Cartesian phase domains, and
   suppose that the projection $z\mapsto(q(z),Q(z))$ onto the old position
   and the new position has invertible derivative at a point $z_{0}$. Then
   there are a neighbourhood of $z_{0}$ and a $C^{3}$ function
   $S:O_{q}\times O_{Q}\to\mathbb R$ with $\det S_{qQ}\neq0$ whose generated
   map agrees with $C$ on that neighbourhood
   ([[prop-cm-canonical-map-locally-has-a-generating-function]]).
4. **(time-dependent generating function)** Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be a
   nonempty open interval and let $S:J\times O_{q}\times O_{Q}\to\mathbb R$
   be of class $C^{3}$ with $\det S_{qQ}(t,q,Q)\neq0$ everywhere; for each
   $t$ let $C_{t}$ be the first-kind map generated by $S_{t}$. Assume the
   values $(q,p)$ used below lie in the domain of $H$ of
   [[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]], and set
   $p:=S_{q}(t,q,Q)$, $P:=-S_{Q}(t,q,Q)$ and
   $K(t,q,Q):=H\bigl(t,q,S_{q}(t,q,Q)\bigr)+\partial_tS(t,q,Q)$. The
   functions $S$ in clauses 1-4 have action dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$;
   in clause 4, $\partial_tS$ has energy dimension
   $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$, so the sum defining $K$ is dimensionally
   consistent. Then:
   (a) each $C_{t}$ is a canonical $C^{2}$ local diffeomorphism of the
   presentation; (b) the Poincare-Cartan identity

$$p\cdot dq-H\,dt=P\cdot dQ-K\,dt+dS$$

   holds on $J\times O_{q}\times O_{Q}$
   ([[prop-cm-time-dependent-generating-function]]); and (c) writing $K$ as
   a function of $(t,Q,P)$ through the correspondence
   $(t,q,Q)\leftrightarrow(t,Q,P)$, a $C^{1}$ curve $t\mapsto(q(t),p(t))$
   satisfies $q'=H_{p}$, $p'=-H_{q}$ if and only if
   $t\mapsto(Q(t),P(t))=C_{t}(q(t),p(t))$ satisfies $Q'=K_{P}$,
   $P'=-K_{Q}$ on the interval where both descriptions are defined.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch, the declared
presentation and the cited mathematics; it asserts no global generating
function, no existence of a canonical map with prescribed data beyond the
local statements, and no empirical content.

**First-kind data.** Let $n\ge1$ and let $O_q,O_Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty open sets
([[def-metric-topology]]). Let $S:O_q\times O_Q\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^3$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) and assume

$$\det S_{qQ}(q,Q)\ne0\qquad\bigl((q,Q)\in O_q\times O_Q\bigr),$$

where $S_{qQ}(q,Q)$ is the $n\times n$ matrix with entries
$\partial^2 S/\partial q^i\partial Q^j(q,Q)$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). Identify $O_q\times O_Q$ with the phase-domain coordinates
$(q,Q)$ of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]) and form the
$C^2$ map

$$\Psi:O_q\times O_Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{2n},\qquad \Psi(q,Q):=\bigl(q,\ S_q(q,Q)\bigr),$$

whose derivative is the block matrix
$D\Psi(q,Q)=\begin{pmatrix}I_n&0\\ S_{qq}(q,Q)&S_{qQ}(q,Q)\end{pmatrix}$. A **generating function of
the first kind** is such an $S$; the **local map generated by $S$** is, on a neighbourhood of a point
$(q_*,Q_*)$, the $C^2$ map $C:(q,p)\mapsto(Q,P)$ defined by

$$p:=S_q(q,Q),\qquad P:=-S_Q(q,Q),$$

solved as follows: since $\det S_{qQ}\ne0$, the inverse function theorem
([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]) makes $\Psi$ a local $C^2$ diffeomorphism, so
$p=S_q(q,Q)$ determines a $C^2$ local inverse $Q=Q(q,p)$ on a neighbourhood of
$\Psi(q_*,Q_*)$; then $C(q,p):=(Q(q,p),-S_Q(q,Q(q,p)))$.

**Second-kind data.** Let $O_q,O_P\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty open sets and let
$S:O_q\times O_P\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^3$ with $\det S_{qP}(q,P)\ne0$ everywhere. A
**generating function of the second kind** is such an $S$; the **local map generated by $S$** is,
near a point $(q_*,P_*)$, the $C^2$ map $C:(q,p)\mapsto(Q,P)$ defined by

$$p:=S_q(q,P),\qquad Q:=S_P(q,P),$$

where again the relation $p=S_q(q,P)$ is solved locally for $P=P(q,p)$ by the inverse function
theorem applied to $(q,P)\mapsto(q,S_q(q,P))$, whose derivative is
$\begin{pmatrix}I_n&0\\ S_{qq}&S_{qP}\end{pmatrix}$.

**Recorded identities.** Wherever $S$ is of the first kind, the identity
$p\,dq-P\,dQ=dS$ holds; wherever $S$ is of the second kind, the identity $p\,dq+Q\,dP=dS$ holds,
both as identities of $C^2$ coordinate one-forms on the $(q,Q)$- resp. $(q,P)$-space with $p,P,Q$ read as the
displayed functions ([[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]]). The mixed-derivative hypotheses
$\det S_{qQ}\ne0$ resp. $\det S_{qP}\ne0$ are part of the data.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $S$ be a generating function of the first kind or of the second kind, with data
$O_q,O_Q$ resp. $O_q,O_P$ and the local map $C$ it generates
([[def-cm-generating-function-of-the-first-and-second-kind]]). Then $C$ is a $C^2$ local
diffeomorphism and it is canonical: on its domain,

$$C^*\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n dQ^i\wedge dP_i\Bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^n dq^i\wedge dp_i .$$

Moreover $|\det DC|=1$ wherever $C$ is defined
([[prop-cm-canonical-map-tests-and-hamiltonian-transport]]).

The words canonical and the finite-regularity form operations here use [[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]], with the displayed $C^2$ maps; smoothness is not inferred.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ and nonempty open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$,
a $C^{2}$ potential $U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ of dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing regularity
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]], the Euclidean product on $\mathbb R^{3N}$ is
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Write $n:=3N\ge1$. The
Cartesian momentum phase chart of the presentation is
$I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with the momentum $p=\mathsf Mv$ of
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]], and the momentum phase chart of a
generalized-coordinate map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates is
$I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ with the generalized momentum
$P=G(q)v$, $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]).

**(a) Cartesian chart.** The **Cartesian phase domain of the presentation** is
the nonempty open set

$$W:=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n},\qquad z=(x,p),$$

a phase domain in the sense of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]
(openness is clause (a) of [[def-cm01-configuration]]; nonemptiness is an
explicit hypothesis here, so an empty configuration domain has no instances
of this phase-domain definition). On $W$ the
**canonical one-form of the presentation in the Cartesian chart** is the smooth
one-form

$$\lambda_{(x,p)}(\delta x,\delta p):=p\cdot\delta x\qquad\bigl((x,p)\in W,\ (\delta x,\delta p)\in\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}\bigr),$$

where $p\cdot\delta x$ is the Euclidean pairing of the momentum covector with
the displacement, and the **two-form of the presentation in the Cartesian
chart** is

$$\omega:=-d\lambda$$

([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]). In coordinates, reading
$x=(x^{1},\dots,x^{3N})$ and $p=(p_{1},\dots,p_{3N})$ as the standard
coordinates of $W$,

$$\lambda=\sum_{a=1}^{3N}p_{a}\,dx^{a},\qquad \omega=\sum_{a=1}^{3N}dx^{a}\wedge dp_{a},\qquad \omega_{(x,p)}\bigl((\delta x,\delta p),(\delta x',\delta p')\bigr)=\delta x\cdot\delta p'-\delta p\cdot\delta x',$$

the last identity using the Euclidean product. The dimension of both forms is
that of action, $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$: the pairing of a momentum
($\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$) with a displacement ($\ell$). The forms have no
explicit time dependence; for each $t\in I_{0}$ the slice $\{t\}\times W$
carries the same two-form. The momentum phase chart with time,
$I_{0}\times W$ with coordinates $(t,x,p)$, is the domain of the Hamiltonians
and fields of this page. The **sign convention** fixed by
[[def-hamiltonian-vector-field-and-hamiltonian-function]] and used
throughout is $\iota_{X}\omega=dH$; $H$ denotes a phase function as in that
item.

**(b) Generalized-coordinate chart.** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
generalized-coordinate map with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$ and
kinetic metric $G$, and let $r$ be its number of coordinates
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]). The **chart map of the
presentation in the coordinates $X$** is

$$\Phi_{X}:\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Phi_{X}(q,P):=\Bigl(X(q),\ \mathsf M\,DX(q)\,G(q)^{-1}P\Bigr).$$

Here $DX(q)$ is the $(3N)\times r$ Jacobian of $X$ at $q$
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]), $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$
is symmetric positive definite ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]],
[[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]), and $P$ is a
generalized momentum. The image of $\Phi_{X}$ is

$$\Phi_{X}(\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r})=\bigl\{\,(X(q),\mathsf M\,DX(q)v)\ :\ q\in\Omega,\ v\in\mathbb R^{r}\,\bigr\},$$

the momentum chart of the presentation in the coordinates $X$; indeed
$P\mapsto v=G(q)^{-1}P$ is a linear bijection of $\mathbb R^{r}$. The map
$\Phi_X$ is $C^2$: $X$ is $C^3$, so $DX$ is $C^2$; hence
$G=DX^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M DX$ is $C^2$, and $G^{-1}$ is $C^2$ because
matrix inversion is given by the adjugate divided by the nonvanishing
determinant on the positive-definite matrices. The fiber
coefficient $\mathsf M DX(q)G(q)^{-1}$ is $C^2$. Thus $\Phi_X$ is a
$C^2$ immersion:
its derivative is injective at every point, because $DX(q)$ is injective
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-euclidean-submersions-and-immersions]]) and $P\mapsto G(q)^{-1}P$ is a
linear bijection; when $r=3N$ its derivative is invertible and it is a local
$C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its open image in $W$
(equivalently $\mathsf M\,DX(q)G(q)^{-1}=DX(q)^{-\mathsf T}$: see the
recorded identity below). We use the pointwise coordinate pullback: for a smooth
$k$-form $\eta$ on $W$, set
$(\Phi_X^*\eta)_{(q,P)}(v_1,\dots,v_k):=
\eta_{\Phi_X(q,P)}(D\Phi_X(q,P)v_1,\dots,D\Phi_X(q,P)v_k)$, extending the
formula of [[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]] to this $C^2$ map. The
result has continuous coefficients. The **forms of the presentation in the
coordinates $X$** are

$$\lambda_{X}:=\Phi_{X}^{*}\lambda,\qquad \omega_{X}:=\Phi_{X}^{*}\omega$$

([[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]]). In the coordinates $(q,P)$ on
$\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ the following identities hold, and are proved in
clause 2 of the symplectic-structure theorem of this page:

$$\lambda_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}P_{a}\,dq^{a},\qquad \omega_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}dq^{a}\wedge dP_{a};$$

moreover, when $r=3N$ and $DX(q)$ is invertible,
$\mathsf M\,DX(q)G(q)^{-1}=DX(q)^{-\mathsf T}$, so that on an open
generalized-coordinate chart the chart map reads
$\Phi_X(q,P)=\bigl(X(q),DX(q)^{-\mathsf T}P\bigr)$ and the chart transition
between the two descriptions of the same momentum datum is a $C^2$ local
diffeomorphism.

**(c) Status.** The item defines the two-form datum of the declared
presentation on its declared charts, together with the sign convention for
fields. It asserts no closedness, no nondegeneracy, no equation of motion, no
conservation law and no measured value; those are the subject of the other
items of this page. The forms depend on the declared chart and its coordinate
dimensions, but not on the residual forces $d$ nor on the normalization
$U\mapsto U+c(t)$ of the potential representative. All objects are model
objects of the idealization declared by the force branch.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data, charts and forms of [[def-cm13-two-form]]: masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$,
open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ and mass operator
$\mathsf M$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), time window $I_{0}$, $C^{2}$
potential $U$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing regularity
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], [[def-cm01-units]]), the Cartesian phase
domain $W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with $n=3N$, its canonical one-form
$\lambda$ and two-form $\omega=-d\lambda$, and for each generalized-coordinate
map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r$ coordinates and kinetic metric $G$ the chart map
$\Phi_{X}(q,P)=(X(q),\mathsf M\,DX(q)G(q)^{-1}P)$ with pullbacks
$\lambda_{X}=\Phi_{X}^{*}\lambda$ and $\omega_{X}=\Phi_{X}^{*}\omega$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]], [[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]). Then:

1. **(Cartesian chart)** $\omega$ is the standard two-form of the phase
   domain $W$ in the sense of
   [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]: $d\omega=0$ and
   $\omega$ is nondegenerate at every point of $W$; hence $(W,\omega)$ is a
   symplectic manifold in the sense of
   [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]].
2. **(generalized-coordinate chart)** On $\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$,

$$\lambda_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}P_{a}\,dq^{a},\qquad \omega_{X}=\sum_{a=1}^{r}dq^{a}\wedge dP_{a};$$

   consequently $\omega_{X}$ is closed and nondegenerate at every point, so
   $\Phi_{X}^{*}\omega$ is the standard two-form of the phase domain
   $\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ and $\Phi_{X}$ preserves the two-form.
3. **(full-dimensional chart transitions)** Let $X_1,X_2$ be generalized-coordinate
   charts with $r=3N$, and restrict their momentum chart maps to neighborhoods
   on which each $\Phi_{X_j}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of the
   Cartesian phase domain. On every overlap of those image neighborhoods,
   the genuine phase-chart transition
   $\Theta=\Phi_{X_2}^{-1}\circ\Phi_{X_1}$ preserves the two-form. The
   difference $\lambda_{X_1}-\Theta^*\lambda_{X_2}$ is a closed one-form

The statement is a conditional deduction from the adopted force branch, the

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with the
momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]], the canonical
coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]] and the Hamiltonian fields of
[[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]]
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]). Let $W_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{2m_j}$ be
nonempty open subsets of phase domains of the presentation, carrying their
respective two-forms $\omega_j$ from [[def-cm13-two-form]] (for a
generalized-coordinate domain this is the pulled-back form $\omega_X$ in its
own $(q,P)$ coordinates). The dimensions $2m_1$ and $2m_2$ need not agree.

**(a) Pullback-preserving maps and transformations.** A $C^{1}$ map
$C:W_{1}\to W_{2}$ is a **canonical map of the presentation** when

$$C^{*}\omega_{2}=\omega_{1}\qquad\text{on }W_{1}$$

with pointwise pullback as in [[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]]. In
standard phase coordinates this is the dimension-aware matrix identity

$$DC(z)^{\mathsf T}J_{m_2}DC(z)=J_{m_1},$$

where $DC(z)$ is a $2m_2\times2m_1$ matrix and
$J_m=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_m\\-I_m&0\end{pmatrix}$. It forces $DC(z)$ to be
injective: if $DC(z)v=0$, then $v^{\mathsf T}J_{m_1}w=0$ for every $w$, so
$v=0$ by nondegeneracy of $J_{m_1}$, so $m_1\le m_2$. Thus it is a $C^1$
immersion preserving the symplectic forms (a symplectic immersion). If it is
also a $C^1$ embedding of the underlying
manifolds (injective and a homeomorphism onto its image), call it a
**canonical embedding**; pullback preservation alone asserts no global
injectivity or topological embedding.

When $m_1=m_2$, a canonical map is automatically a local diffeomorphism by
the inverse function theorem; call it a **local canonical transformation**.
A **canonical transformation** is a canonical map that is a $C^1$
diffeomorphism onto $W_2$. The same-dimensional definitions agree with the
finite-regularity convention of
[[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]]; the $C^\infty$ case agrees
with [[def-canonical-transformation]] and
[[def-symplectomorphism-local-symplectomorphism-and-symplectic-embedding]].
The different-dimensional definition here extends those finite-coordinate
notions only by the displayed pullback equality.

**(b) Equal-dimensional matrix and determinant tests.** If $m_1=m_2=m$,
then by [[prop-cm-canonical-map-tests-and-hamiltonian-transport]] clause 1
the pullback condition is equivalent to

$$DC(z)^{\mathsf T}J_m\,DC(z)=J_m\qquad\text{for every }z\in W_{1}.$$

The derivative is invertible at every point, so the map is a local
diffeomorphism by [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]. Taking
determinants of the matrix identity gives $(\det DC(z))^2=1$, hence
$|\det DC(z)|=1$ for every $z$
([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]],
[[cor-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-is-a-unit]],
[[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]). In dimension $2m\ge4$ the condition
$|\det DC|=1$ alone is strictly weaker than canonicity (the companion page
carries an explicit volume-preserving, non-canonical shear), while for $m=1$ the symplectic condition is exactly $\det DC=1$; absolute determinant $1$ alone also admits orientation-reversing, antisymplectic maps.
If $m_1\ne m_2$, $DC$ is rectangular, so no square determinant test is
defined; the dimension-aware pullback identity of clause (a) is the criterion.

**(c) Elementary closure and equal-dimensional field transport.** By
pointwise functoriality of pullback, the identity map, composites of
composable canonical maps and inverses of canonical transformations are
canonical. For a $C^{2}$ equal-dimensional canonical map
$C:W_{1}\to W_{2}$ and a $C^{2}$ function $f$ on $W_{2}$, the Hamiltonian
fields satisfy

$$DC(z)\,X_{f\circ C}(z)=X_{f}\bigl(C(z)\bigr)\qquad(z\in W_{1}),$$

so that $C$ conjugates the Hamiltonian system of $f\circ C$ to that of $f$
by the chain rule and the equal-dimensional matrix identity: taking the
inverse of $DC^{\mathsf T}J_mDC=J_m$ gives $DCJ_mDC^{\mathsf T}=J_m$, which
substituted into $DCJ_m\nabla(f\circ C)$ yields the displayed identity. No
such ambient field-transport identity is asserted for a lower-dimensional
symplectic immersion: the ambient field need not be tangent to its image.
Bracket, solution and phase-volume consequences are likewise limited to
their stated equal-dimensional local transformations.

**(d) The model's canonical maps.** For every generalized-coordinate
immersion $X$, the momentum map $\Phi_X$ in [[def-cm13-two-form]] is a
dimension-aware canonical map by clause 2 of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]]; it is a symplectic immersion and is not
asserted to be a global embedding. When $r=3N$, its local branches and the
genuine transitions between such charts are equal-dimensional local
canonical transformations by clauses 2-3 of that theorem. The drift, kick and velocity-Verlet maps of the mechanical splitting in exact
arithmetic are equal-dimensional local canonical transformations on their
admissible domains whenever those domains are nonempty, by
[[prop-cm-drift-kick-and-verlet-preserve-the-canonical-form]].

**(e) Status.** The item defines the canonical maps of the presentation and
fixes the dimension-aware pullback test of clause (a) and the equal-dimensional
matrix test of clause (b). It asserts no existence of a canonical map beyond
the listed suppliers, no global statement on multiply connected phase domains
and no empirical content; in particular, canonicity is a local condition on
the two-form, and an equal-dimensional canonical transformation need not admit
a globally defined real generating function, as the scope remark of this page
records.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth, and let $\omega\in\Omega^k(N)$. The **pullback**
$F^*\omega$ is the pullback of $\omega$ viewed as an alternating covariant
$k$-tensor field:

$$ (F^*\omega)_p(v_1,\ldots,v_k)=\omega_{F(p)}(dF_pv_1,\ldots,dF_pv_k). $$

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the **transpose** of $A$ is the matrix
$A^{\mathsf T}\in M_{n\times m}(F)$ defined by

$$(A^{\mathsf T})_{ji}:=a_{ij}.$$

Thus transposition interchanges rows and columns. The transpose of a zero-sized
matrix is the unique matrix of the transposed zero-sized shape.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

A matrix $A\in M_n(F)$ is **invertible** when there is a matrix $B\in M_n(F)$
such that

$$AB=I_n=BA.$$

Such a $B$ is unique and is denoted $A^{-1}$. The **general linear set** is

$$\operatorname{GL}_n(F):=\{A\in M_n(F):A\text{ is invertible}\}.$$

It is the set of units of the ring $M_n(F)$. The fact that it is a group under
matrix multiplication is [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]. For $n=0$,
the unique empty matrix is $I_0$ and is its own inverse.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $n\geq1$, and $A\in M_n(R)$. Then $A$ is
invertible if and only if $\det(A)$ is a unit of $R$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: The displayed curve has $\dot x=m^{-1}p$ and $\dot p=0$, hence solves the Hamiltonian system for all $t$, so by the solutions clause of [F1] it is the free-particle flow; this is claim 1.

Mixed Hessian and generated map: $S_{t,q}(q,Q)=-\frac{m}{2t}\cdot2(Q-q)\cdot(-1)=\frac{m}{t}(Q-q)$, so $S_{t,qQ}=\frac{m}{t}I_{3}$ is invertible for $t\neq0$; the first-kind relations of [F2] read $p=S_{t,q}=\frac{m}{t}(Q-q)$ and $P=-S_{t,Q}=\frac{m}{t}(Q-q)=p$, hence $Q=q+\frac{t}{m}p$ and $P=p$: the generated map is $\Phi_{t}$; by [F2] it is canonical with unit determinant, which is claim 2.

Projection and degeneration: the derivative of $(q,p)\mapsto(q,Q)$ is the displayed block matrix with invertible diagonal blocks $I_{3}$ and $(t/m)I_{3}$ for $t\neq0$, so the projection is invertible there; at $t=0$ the function $S_{t}$ is undefined and the lower-right block vanishes, so the projection is singular, and no member of the family represents the identity map; this is claim 3.

Pullback of the one-form: $\Phi_{t}^{*}\lambda=P\cdot dQ$ with $Q=q+(t/m)p$ and $P=p$, so $\Phi_{t}^{*}\lambda=p\cdot(dq+(t/m)dp)=\lambda+(t/m)\,d\bigl(\lvert p\rvert^{2}/2\bigr)=\lambda+t\,dK$ by the chain rule and the symmetry of the Euclidean product [F3]; differentiating gives $\Phi_{t}^{*}d\lambda=d\lambda$, and the matrix identity of claim 2 was already computed; this is claim 4.
Collecting steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2 proves the four claims on the declared data.
